title: Audi and NVIDIA Use Agile Robots for Parts Sequencing Trial
content:
Audi and NVIDIA Use Agile Robots for Parts Sequencing Trial
Prioritise Us
on Google
Audi is working with Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA to automate parts sequencing at its Ingolstadt plant using mobile humanoid robots. Credit: Audi
Audi’s Board Member for Production and Logistics Gerd Walker explains how Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA are bringing physical AI to logistics
Audi is working with Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA to automate parts sequencing at its Ingolstadt plant using mobile humanoid robots. The proof of concept targets one of automotive logistics’ most complex activities: picking mixed components and placing them in the correct order for vehicle assembly.
Audi targets humanoid robotics for parts sequencing
Audi’s demand-driven material supply operation manages approximately one million picks every day, ensuring that the correct parts reach the correct workstation in the correct assembly sequence.
The partners are testing mobile humanoids in Audi’s Production Lab, an innovation environment for future manufacturing and logistics technologies. The robots are picking components from material containers and place them into sequence for the final assembly of Audi premium vehicles. The initial trials were undertaken in spring 2025 before more in-depth technical developments began in summer 2025. Three robots are taking part in the current trial.
The project brings together Audi’s production and supply-chain expertise; Agile Robots’ mobile humanoid robotics; Dassault Systèmes’ DELMIA virtual-twin technology; and NVIDIA’s physical-AI and robotics libraries.
The proof-of-concept project is designed to test whether humanoid robots can automate high-variant logistics tasks while fitting into existing factory environments.
“The future of manufacturing will be defined by how successfully we combine industrial expertise with artificial intelligence. For decades, picking within the sequencing process has remained one of the toughest automation challenges in automotive logistics," says Gerd Walker, Member of the Board of Management for Production and Logistics at Audi.
"Together with our partners, we are now exploring how AI-powered robotics can help solve this challenge and unlock a new level of productivity in our Audi factories."
The proof of concept project does not have a specified completion date. "The project is ongoing, with Agile Robots and Audi continuing to develop, optimise and evaluate the solution. As always with the goal to get the solution into series production as quickly as possible with a given ROI," an Audi spokesperson confirms.
Gerd Walker, Member of the Board of Management for Production and Logistics, Audi AG. Credit: Audi AG
Virtual twin validates robot deployment
The project has a wider focus than simply demonstrating for the first time that the repetitive and complex picking process, which is currently performed manually, can be automated.
Before the mobile humanoids are deployed in Audi’s smart intralogistics environment, the partners are creating a virtual twin of the logistics operation using Dassault Systèmes' DELMIA application.
"What we can say is that this Proof of Concept and further projects contribute to several broader objectives," an Audi spokesperson explains, adding
With the help of the virtual twin, we are laying the foundation for significantly faster planning processes and the future scaling of AI robotics applications."
The virtual twin can significantly accelerate production planning:
In the future, Audi aims to virtually simulate, test and optimise new layouts, for example the logistics setup for a new model, and train the associated AI robotics virtually before implementing them in the physical factory. Planning processes that can take weeks or even months today could thus be reduced to just a few days. Feasibility, cycle times, ergonomics and safety can also be validated virtually at an early stage.
The virtual twin is a key enabler for scaling AI robotics:
In addition to real-world training data, large volumes of virtual training data can be generated across a wide range of scenarios. This data foundation enables AI models to be specifically trained and optimised to meet the demanding requirements for success rates and availability in high-volume production.
The technological foundation
is the interaction between Dassault Systèmes’ DELMIA Virtual Twin and NVIDIA Omniverse: DELMIA creates a virtual representation of the production and logistics environment, while NVIDIA technologies support physics-based simulations and Physical AI applications, among other capabilities.
Agile Robots brings mobile humanoids to the factory
Munich-based Agile Robots says it has deployed more than 20,000 robotic solutions worldwide. The trial features mobile humanoid robots, which combine humanoid reach and dexterity with the robustness of a mobile base. The robots are a new product that has just been developed by the robotics developer. The robots operate at human height, and feature dual-arm manipulation and a mobile base.
The design is intended to help the robots work alongside existing equipment and infrastructure, rather than requiring a complete redesign of Audi’s intralogistics environment.
“Agile Robots is driving industries forward with physical AI. Working with Audi we show how our mobile humanoids can perform high-value, critical tasks that were previously impossible to automate. That is what physical AI is all about – real progress for industrial productivity,” says Dr Zhaopeng Chen, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Agile Robots.
Physical AI targets complex logistics tasks
Traditional industrial robots are highly effective when operating in structured environments with predictable components, fixed positions and repeatable movements. Automotive parts sequencing is more difficult because components can vary in size, shape, packaging and location.
The proof of concept focuses on two persistent automation challenges: handling high-variant or semi-rigid parts, and picking unsorted components from mixed containers.
Agile Robots’ dual-arm mobile humanoids are designed to handle larger and more flexible components. AI-powered perception allows the systems to identify, grasp and manipulate parts presented in different positions and packaging formats.
The partners describe this as a step towards the introduction of physical AI powered humanoid robotics into high-volume manufacturing. Physical AI refers to systems that combine artificial intelligence with perception, motion, manipulation and interaction with the physical world.
The proof of concept targets one of automotive logistics’ most complex activities: picking mixed components and placing them in the correct order for vehicle assembly. Credit: Audi AG
NVIDIA supports simulation and edge AI
NVIDIA is contributing its robotics and physical AI technologies to the project. Its Omniverse libraries are being used within Dassault Systèmes’ virtual twin environment to simulate and validate the robot’s activities before physical deployment.
NVIDIA also provides robotics software and accelerated computing technologies used to support perception, simulation and edge AI. The company announced that Agile Robots’ Agile ONE SN reference humanoid is preconfigured with NVIDIA Isaac GR00T and powered by the NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge-AI platform.
“Humanoid robots are advancing automation beyond fixed, repetitive tasks to the complex, variable work at the heart of modern manufacturing," says Deepu Talla, NVIDIA’s Vice President of Robotics and Edge AI.
Dassault Systèmes accelerates factory engineering
Dassault Systèmes is providing the digital engineering layer for the project through DELMIA and the 3DEXPERIENCE platform.
Philippe Laufer, Executive Vice President of 3DS Global Brands at Dassault Systèmes, says the main breakthrough was not simply bringing humanoid robots into factories, but validating their tasks before physical deployment.
The platform is intended to allow engineering teams to:
model the production environment
simulate robot missions
test timing and feasibility
evaluate worker ergonomics
validate safety requirements
use physical AI libraries
reduce commissioning risk.
This virtual-first approach is particularly relevant to automotive manufacturers, where production changes can affect highly synchronised assembly operations. The introduction of robots into discrete tasks, such as the picking of mixed components and parts sequencing, would not introduce significant disruption into the series production of automobiles.

title: Greater range at the same weight: silicon battery passes laboratory test - electrive.com
content:
A critical breakthrough in battery research saw film cells with silicon-rich anodes endure over 1,000 cycles in testing without dropping below 80 per cent capacity. We explore the parameters that play a key role and what this progress could mean for electric vehicles.
Image: Fraunhofer ISE
Researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE) have successfully operated a self-manufactured 25-Ah pouch cell with silicon-rich anodes for over 1,000 full cycles as part of the ‘StrOboBatt’ project. After testing, the cell retained more than 83 per cent of its capacity. This achievement marks an important milestone in battery development: 1,000 full cycles with at least 80 per cent capacity retention are considered the minimum requirement for commercial use.
Silicon: high energy density, but extreme expansion
The pouch cell stands out due to its silicon-rich anode, which enables higher energy density compared to conventional graphite anodes. However, silicon has not yet been widely adopted as an anode material because its volume expands by up to 300 per cent (quadrupling) during charging due to lithium-ion absorption and then shrinks again during discharging. This significant movement leads to the loss of electrical contact within the electrode and accelerates the decomposition of the electrolyte. As a result, the cell degrades too quickly for practical use. By comparison, graphite expands by only about 10 to 12 per cent.
To reduce the mechanical stress caused by this extreme expansion, the researchers at Fraunhofer ISE used a silicon-carbon composite, which accounts for 51 per cent of the anode’s active material. Combined with a nickel-rich cathode, the pouch cell was produced on an industry-scale pilot line.
Pressure and charging dynamics are key factors
In the laboratory, the battery cell prototypes were also subjected to an axial pressure of 1,000 kilopascals (approx. 10 bar) during charging and discharging. Despite the material’s movement, the electrode contact remained stable. At a lower pressure of 300 kilopascals (approx. 3 bar), however, the usable capacity decreased significantly faster. Thus, external mechanical pressure proved to be a decisive parameter.
Tests under dynamic real-world conditions also showed that usable capacity declines more rapidly at high power levels than during gentle test cycles. This provides an important insight for future use in electric vehicles, whose battery management systems must account for this factor.
The tested cells achieved a gravimetric energy density of 280 Wh/kg. However, Fraunhofer ISE states that industrially optimised mass production could achieve around 330 Wh/kg. A battery with 330 Wh/kg would represent an increase of approx. 20 to 35 per cent compared to today’s NMC and NCA cells and almost double the energy density of LFP cells.
European raw materials for greater range
In practical terms, this means that an electric vehicle could carry nearly 100 kWh of storage capacity instead of today’s approximately 75 kWh at the same battery weight. This would increase the realistic range of a mid-sized vehicle from around 450 km to well over 600 km.
In addition to the range increase, the technology offers a strategic advantage for the industrial sector. Since graphite is currently imported primarily from outside Europe, the increased use of silicon composites enables a partial shift in raw material value creation to Europe, as silicon can be sourced and produced synthetically on a regional basis.

title: CATL's Akin Li: "Whichever battery type the market demands, we'll have it" - electrive.com
content:
Image: Cora Werwitzke
Executive President of CATL’s Overseas Business
Akin Li is a senior executive at CATL and responsible for the company’s international business development. In this role, Li oversees, among other things, the establishment of strategic partnerships and the global market expansion of the company. Before joining CATL, Li held leading positions in the smartphone and consumer electronics industry for over a decade.
Interview
CATL is a near-indispensable supplier to the emerging European e-truck industry, with many model series from local manufacturers running on cells or entire battery packs from the Chinese company. We met with CATL’s top manager Akin Li to explore how CATL plans to further strengthen its partnerships with Europe’s truck manufacturers.
‘CATL’ – these four letters are engraved on the battery packs of many electric trucks. This is the case not only in China, but also here in Europe, where the Ningde-based company supplies truck manufacturers with both the cells and the complete batteries that sit at the heart of every electrified vehicle. What’s more, the pace of development remains unabated: just this week, CATL introduced another
battery innovation for heavy-duty trucks
in China, based on its own battery-swapping technology. While this approach remains uncommon in Europe, CATL sees clear potential for it here as well.
With this in mind, we spoke with CATL’s top executive for international business about the company’s localisation plans for Europe as well as the fundamental debate between NMC and LFP. In the conversation with electrive editor Cora Werwitzke, we also discussed the distinct differences between customers and markets in China and Europe. First and foremost: CATL certainly recognises the challenges that the path to electrification presents for all industry players here. But Li and his team prefer to focus sharply on the opportunities that lie beyond.
Mr. Li, CATL manufactures batteries for both passenger cars and trucks. What’s the secret to a good truck battery?
Well, when it comes to safety, there are some basic requirements that must be met. Safety is fundamental, together with liability and longevity. Those are the basics – regardless of whether the batteries are for electric trucks or electric cars. For passenger cars, however, factors such as battery cost and weight may play less of a role than they do for trucks. With commercial vehicles, we’re talking about a work tool, and the fleet operators who purchase them want to turn a profit. It often comes down to the TCO of the vehicle in general and the battery in particular. So that is what we are focused on.
When we look at European electric trucks, we get the impression that hardly any brand can do without CATL anymore. Mercedes, MAN, Scania, DAF – the list of local customers is extensive.
Well, we are glad to support every customer. At IAA Transportation, our CEO Robin Zeng met with Volvo Group CEO Martin [Volvo Group CEO Martin Lundstedt], since we’ve already agreed to collaborate. So I expect that the Volvo Group will also be using CATL batteries in the coming years.
CATL manufactures battery cells based on both NMC and LFP chemistries. In your opinion, will the trend in commercial vehicles eventually swing in favour of one of these in the long term?
We produce NMC cells, and we also have LFP and even sodium-ion batteries. So, in terms of chemical composition, we’re trying to offer a variety of options. Just recently, we discussed your question with an OEM – looking ahead to the next ten years. To be honest, we don’t know which chemistry will be the best around the year 2035. What we can say is this: no matter which one turns out to be the best – CATL will have it ready; whether it’s NMC, LFP, sodium-ion, entirely different chemistries, or solid-state – even if the latter is still a long way off. In short, we’re not focusing on a single specific chemistry for all commercial vehicles. The application areas are already very diverse, as are the usage scenarios as well. We simply work closely with the OEMs and deliver the best solution for each specific application. That’s the logic.
In China, LFP batteries are said to be ubiquitous in trucks by now.
Actually, it’s because most electric trucks in China operate on short distances, fixed routes, and at high utilisation rates. Trucks in China are often in service 24 hours a day and don’t take long breaks. Therefore, a long life cycle is important. For this reason, LFP is preferred. However, for certain applications – such as long-distance transport – very fast charging times and a longer range are required. So, if you’re shipping very expensive seafood or the iPhone 18 over long distances, where cost is less of a factor, then you probably need the high energy density of NMC.
Do customer expectations differ in Europe?
Well, in China, a truck’s life is somewhat shorter. They’re usually sold after four or five years. In Europe, on the other hand, customers want a truck to remain in service for at least eight to ten years. What many people may not know is that in China, there are a lot of private individuals who own trucks. They want to recoup their investment as quickly as possible. In Europe, however, there are large fleets and major operators. They tend to focus on long-term returns. That’s a key difference.
Talking about differences: why is the electic truck market in China already so much more mature than in Europe?
There are many differences between the markets. In the typical scenario in China, the charging infrastructure – whether it involves charging stations or battery-swap stations – is easy to set up thanks to the short distances and fixed routes. In Europe, the focus is more on the broader transportation sector, particularly long-distance transport. Routes often cross through different countries with varying regulations, which makes things more complex.
However, I believe that beyond these differences, there are primarily commonalities. For example, we are currently working with DHL. They, too, want to reduce CO2 emissions. And they are willing to take a leading role in Europe in establishing a ‘green corridor’. We also have such customers in China that are striving to reduce CO2 emissions. So I think the electrification goals are identical for both regions. The difference, however, is that China is a unified market. We have one government, one policy, and one set of regulations. So, if you decide to do something, you just need to get one proof, and it is okay. Here, on the other hand, we’re dealing with cross-border issues, and you have to, let’s say, hold many discussions with various parties.
So what does CATL’s future strategy for Europe look like – including your plans for localisation? MAN already receives your NMC cells from Erfurt, Germany, but the LFP batteries – for Daimler Truck, for example – are imported from China, right?
We’re currently manufacturing in China. But as you mentioned regarding Erfurt, the plant there is already supplying cells to MAN. So that’s a level of flexibility we can use – and are currently using. In general, we have three plants in Europe. In addition to Erfurt, these include factories in Hungary and Spain, the latter as a joint venture. Overall, capacity will total more than 150 gigawatts and will include both NMC and LFP batteries. So if local production becomes necessary for trucks here, we’ll be right there. We’re relying on a very flexible strategy in collaboration with the OEMs. In the long term, however, a lot depends on the market situation.
What about battery swap systems? They’re a big topic in China. Does this technology also have potential in Europe?
If you look at the situation in China five years ago, people there had serious doubts – just like in Europe today. But battery swapping has since become one of the most important options for customers in China. That’s because it gives them the choice to buy their vehicle with or without a battery. According to current market data, we know that for some passenger car brands, the majority of customers lease the battery. Why? Because buyers of electric cars used to have major concerns about their vehicle’s depreciation. And above all, they didn’t trust the battery. Swapping technology separates the previously inseparable unit of car and battery. And of course, this approach reduces the initial cost: after all, the battery accounts for nearly 25 to 30 per cent of the vehicle’s price.
Which amounts to even more money when it comes to trucks…
Yes, it’s the same with trucks. In China, many private truck owners are carefully considering whether it might be better to lease the battery so they can afford an electric truck more quickly. But in Europe, in my opinion, it’s not primarily about the costs. It’s more about the infrastructure. Whether we’re talking with OEMs, operators, or end customers: Everyone is talking about traditional charging and the necessary grid connections. Many complain that this takes too much time. The thing is: for battery swap, we don’t need a high grid connection capacity at all. We charge the batteries slowly and then install them in the vehicle. This can significantly reduce the time needed to set up a charging infrastructure.
Your team says that a battery swap takes just five minutes?
Yes, charging time is another argument. In Europe, you have to take a 45-minute break after a four-and-a-half-hour drive. Conventional fast charging is fine for that. But in reality, when you want to take a break, many other drivers are also taking a break. So you’d rather wait in line at a battery-swap station, where the swap takes five minutes, than wait in line at a charging station where each truck takes 25 minutes.
Do you get the impression that
OEMs here in Europe are interested in this approach? After all, that also means standardising the batteries.
I think they’re interested, but they’re still hesitant. They argue that they have to cover so many use cases and therefore can’t standardise the batteries. But you know, here’s the thing: we believe that, drawing on our experience in China, we can find a solution together. In China, all the automakers also said that their chassis and designs were too different. But we’ve since developed standard battery packs – #20 #25 and #26 for passenger cars, and 75# for heavy-duty trucks – and these can be integrated into 85 per cent of the A-segment models in China. So the OEMs don’t need to worry. If they’re interested, if they want to implement this, then we’ll find a solution.
You appear to see solutions, rather than problems.
We see opportunities beyond the problems, beyond the challenges. There will certainly be many challenges. For example, we’re discussing who will own the batteries and who will be willing to invest in this business, which requires significant capital commitments. But let me be clear: I believe there’s a lot of money just waiting to be invested in a good business. Even gas stations and oil companies want to realign their business strategies for the long term. After all, they can’t rely on gasoline or oil forever. And what will their business look like in 20 years? Perhaps they could invest in batteries and charging stations. There are many possibilities.
Is that the case in China – are gas stations changing their business models already?
Yes, they are. Because with the high number of electric vehicle registrations in China, there are already some gas stations that no longer have enough customers. And so they may start setting up charging stations or battery swap stations. Of course, this doesn’t happen overnight. It’s a gradual transformation.
Mr. Li, thank you very much for the interview.

title: QuantumScape's 100-MWh Line Targets AI Data Centers, Defense
content:

The solid-state battery maker's latest demonstration facility will show its licensing blueprint can scale beyond automotive — and beyond EVs' slowing growth curve.
October 21, 2026
5 Min Read
QuantumScape's San Jose facility
QuantumScape
At a Glance
QuantumScape's new 100-MWh line, to be equipped with Muehlbauer automation, targets AI data centers, aerospace, and defense.
The line is a demonstration facility, not a commercial plant — QuantumScape licenses its technology rather than sells cells.
Cell production is targeted for 2028, extending the Eagle Line blueprint already developed with Volkswagen's PowerCo.
QuantumScape Corporation announced today a planned 100 megawatt-hour capacity cell production line to demonstrate its ability to meet demand for solid-state batteries from AI data centers, aerospace, and defense — markets that didn't register in the company's messaging when it opened its Eagle Line pilot facility just eight months ago. QuantumScape is building the new 100-MWh line itself, with Germany's Muehlbauer Group supplying automation and cell-assembly equipment; Muehlbauer evaluated the Eagle Line's existing processes and designed enhancements to help bring the technology to mass-production throughput. Start of cell production is targeted for 2028.
The news lands amid a broader industry reorientation: battery makers across the sector are redirecting capacity
toward the power appetite of AI infrastructure as EV demand growth cools
. Ford, for one, has begun
converting EV battery capacity toward grid and data-center storage
. But QuantumScape's move is different in kind. It isn't repurposing existing production capacity to sell batteries into a new market — the company doesn't manufacture cells for sale at all. Instead, the new line is a demonstration facility, built to prove that its solid-state chemistry and manufacturing process can be scaled to the throughput and performance levels these markets would demand of a future licensee.
Related:
Battery Show North America 2026: Technology Highlights From the Show Floor
Why solid-state chemistry matters for these markets
QuantumScape's core technology advantage is its ceramic separator — a solid material that replaces the flammable liquid electrolyte found in conventional lithium-ion cells. CTO Tim Holme has described the separator as conducting lithium "
nearly as fast as lithium flows through water
," while delivering the stability and safety characteristics that liquid electrolytes can't match. For data centers and aerospace/defense applications — where thermal runaway risk, energy density, and longevity carry outsized weight — that safety and performance profile is precisely the differentiator Holme has said makes solid-state technology best suited to "applications prioritizing safety or high performance," as opposed to cost-optimized, utility-scale grid storage.
QuantumScape Chief Technology Officer Tim Holme. Credit: M. Anderson / Battery Technology
That distinction matters for how to read today's announcement. QuantumScape isn't chasing the lowest-cost segment of the energy storage market; it's demonstrating that its ceramic-separator chemistry can perform at the scale and quality that premium segments — AI data centers, aerospace, defense — demand, where performance and safety margins justify a higher price than liquid-electrolyte alternatives can offer.
Related:
Inside the 2026 Battery Awards, Where Innovation Took Center Stage
Scaling the Cobra process
The manufacturing side of the story is just as central. QuantumScape's proprietary Cobra process, the method underlying its ceramic separator production, compressed what Holme described in February as a multi-day ceramic-firing step — "like baking pottery," he said — down to a matter of minutes, a breakthrough that took four years of R&D. That speed is what makes gigawatt-hour-scale output economically viable at all: "it's that kind of throughput that is needed to produce at gigawatt hours," Holme said.
Scaling that chemistry into mechanical mass production is a separate challenge, which is exactly what the Eagle Line was built to demonstrate. Holme has framed the leap from benchtop to gigafactory as a "13 orders of magnitude" problem, solvable only through repeated automation improvements — "the remaining scaling requires automation factors of 10, repeated eight times." The Eagle Line,
which went from planning to operation in just ten months
according to CEO Siva Sivaram, was explicitly built not as a path to QuantumScape's own mass production, but as what Holme called "a blueprint for others to follow" — with an estimated 98% of the process directly replicable by future licensees, pending only form-factor-specific tooling adjustments.
Related:
Battery Show Panel Tackles Scaling Energy Storage for Rising Demand
The new Muehlbauer equipped line as the next proof point
Today's announcement extends that demonstration. The new 100-MWh line isn't a separate facility for a separate chemistry; it's built on the same Eagle Line process, with Muehlbauer's automation equipment engineered to push that process to higher throughput. The resulting capacity is what lets QuantumScape demonstrate performance at a scale closer to what data-center and aerospace/defense customers — or the licensees eventually serving them — would require.
This follows the pattern QuantumScape set with Volkswagen's PowerCo, whose two roughly $130 million agreements and embedded engineering team gave QuantumScape its first real-world proof that
the Eagle Line blueprint could transfer to another company's manufacturing operation
, in that case for automotive cells moving through the industry's A-Sample-to-C-Sample development phases.
Muehlbauer's equipment now helps demonstrate that the same blueprint extends to a higher-throughput, higher-volume production tier — the scale-up step needed to show the data-center and aerospace-defense opportunity is reachable, without QuantumScape itself becoming a cell supplier to those markets.
A premium-market strategy, not a volume play
Taken together, the new line reinforces something Holme told us back in February: QuantumScape's founding thesis was that existing lithium-ion technology was "good enough to get early adopters, but not good enough to capture the mass market." With EV penetration still sitting at just 5-10% depending on geography, and solid-state competitors like Factorial Energy also pivoting toward "
defense & aerospace, robotics, and hyperscale data centers
" alongside automotive work, the broader solid-state sector appears to be converging on the same conclusion: the highest-value near-term demonstration opportunity for next-generation battery chemistry may not be the EV itself, but the high-performance, safety-critical applications increasingly defining AI infrastructure and defense procurement.
For QuantumScape, the 100-MWh line isn't a pivot away from automotive — the PowerCo partnership remains very much active — so much as a demonstration that its licensing blueprint can scale in more than one direction at once.

title: Five Takeaways on CATL's Heavy-Duty Truck Batteries
content:
Charging
EV Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Industry Trends
Five takeaways from CATL's latest heavy-duty truck electrification push, covering battery use, battery swapping speed, downtime, flexibility, and commercial fleet operations.
October 21, 2026
4 Min Read
CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026.
Electric heavy-duty trucking electrification is entering a more mature phase. As adoption grows, the conversation is shifting from battery range and charging speed to commercial capability: how well these electric trucks perform in real fleet operations. CATL’s latest announcement moves beyond technical specifications toward the full-lifecycle value of electrifying heavy-duty trucks.
CATL is framing its announcement as a broader response to the operational and economic pressures that still affect electric heavy-duty truck adoption. The five takeaways from the press release show how the company is trying to improve battery utilization, reduce downtime, and build a more flexible commercial model.
CATL is targeting full operating lifecycle
For early electric truck deployments, range, charging speed, and vehicle performance were often the primary benchmarks. CATL is now emphasizing a more mature set of questions: How efficiently is the battery being used? How much downtime does the truck face? How flexible is the cost structure during seasonal demand swings?
Related:
Home EV Chargers Need NEC and UL-Listed 50-Amp EV-Certified Receptacles
The announcement implies that adoption will depend less on demonstrating electrification's technical feasibility and more on demonstrating that it can work economically across the full vehicle lifecycle.
2. The dual-battery design is meant to improve utilization, not just extend range
The central product announcement is CATL’s dual-electric range extension battery, which combines two “independent yet complementary battery systems.” The main battery is the standardized, chassis-mounted
swappable battery
used in the QIJI network. A second battery, mounted behind the cab, acts as a range extender and backup power source. CATL says the current version uses a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging.
In conventional battery-swapping operations, drivers may return for a swap before fully using the main battery because they do not want to risk running too low. CATL says its backup battery raises the main battery’s depth of discharge “from approximately 70% to over 95%,” allowing the vehicle to return with “less than 5% state of charge.
Standardized swapping blocks with the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) units. Courtesy of CATL.
3. CATL is combining standardization with application flexibility
A recurring challenge in heavy-duty transport is that no two operating environments are exactly alike. Route length, payload, climate, and duty cycle all affect what kind of battery system works best. CATL’s response is what it calls a “1+X” architecture.
Under that model, one standardized main battery ensures compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the secondary range-extension battery can be tailored to different operating needs. CATL notes that “the two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently.”
Related:
Honda Introduces In-Motion Charging Technology for Large Commercial EVs
That matters because scale in freight infrastructure usually requires standardization, and CATL is trying to argue that the sector does not need to choose between the two.
QIJI battery-swapping station. Courtesy of CATL.
4. QIJI’s battery-swapping strategy is built around operational speed and cost structure
The announcement also shows that CATL sees swapping as more than a faster way to refuel. QIJI’s model is being presented as a full operating system for heavy-duty electrification. The company says its network can complete battery swaps “in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate.” It has also expanded standardized swapping blocks with the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) units alongside the existing 75# block.
On the commercial side, QIJI is pushing flexible battery ownership and leasing arrangements. CATL says the onboard range-extension battery remains with the truck as a long-term asset, while the main swappable battery can be leased based on freight demand. QIJI has also introduced a battery-as-a-service model in which customers pay “for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged,” allowing them to retain the value of regenerative braking. According to the release, this can reduce “per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%.”
Related:
EV Charging Demand Outpaces Infrastructure Growth, Signaling Market Shift for Charge Station Operators
Chassis-mounted long-range battery. Courtesy of CATL.
5. The scale ambitions are large, and CATL is signaling early market traction
CATL used the announcement to underscore scale. It says it plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026, 2,000 by 2027, and ultimately 10,000 stations nationwide with partners. Those are ambitious numbers, but they reflect a clear understanding that long-haul freight electrification depends on network confidence, not just vehicle capability.
The company also pointed to agreements signed for 13,000 units at the event, suggesting meaningful commercial interest already exists. Jesse Yang, CEO of QIJI Energy, summarized the company’s position directly: “The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and QIJI battery swapping offers the best solution for electrifying heavy-duty trucks.”

Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. During her internship at Pequiven S.A. in Venezuela, she trained neural networks using MATLAB (Kohonen Map) to estimate electrical circuit variables for oil wells (e.g., voltage, current, and power).
In addition to her engineering roles, Guerra worked as a freelance technical editor, refining complex technical content for clarity and accuracy. She later became a Power/Analog Editor at

title: How PepsiCo Is Scaling Green Pilots For APAC Supply Chains
content:
How PepsiCo Is Scaling Green Pilots For APAC Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
PepsiCo Greenhouse Programme APAC 2026: The IMPACT Edition aims to prepare pilots for deployment into day-to-day operations. Credit: PepsiCo
"Sustainability and resilience are increasingly linked," Ashley Brown, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo, tells Supply Chain Digital
has announced the next steps for its PepsiCo Greenhouse Programme APAC 2026: The IMPACT Edition, an accelerator designed to equip sustainable pilots for practical deployment across supply chains.
The company has signed five letters of intent with returning alumni to explore future integration across PepsiCo’s Asia Pacific operations.
“What's exciting about these solutions is that many of them can support both sustainability goals and business resilience at the same time,” Ashley Brown, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo APAC, tells Supply Chain Digital. “That's where we see the greatest opportunity for the APAC Greenhouse program.”
Ashley Brown, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo APAC. Credit: PepsiCo
PepsiCo’s selected pilots at a glance:
Adiona, an Australian technology company using AI to optimise logistics networks, route planning and fleet efficiency.
Bali Waste Cycle, an Indonesian startup focused on flexible packaging recovery, plastic recycling and circular economy solutions.
Beijing AIForce, a Chinese agricultural technology company developing electric tractors and low-emission farm machinery.
Takachar, a Thai startup converting agricultural waste into biochar for potential use across agricultural value chains.
X-Centric Sciences, an Australia-based company supporting soil health monitoring and precision agriculture.
How supply chains can move pilots into deployment
Unveiled in May 2026, the IMPACT Edition of PepsiCO’s Greenhouse Programme introduced a new framework to a scheme initially launched in 2023.
Building on the programme’s three previous runs, designed to support startups through testing phases, the IMPACT Edition aims to equip them for deployment into supply chains’ day-to-day operations.
For supply chain leaders, tackling the gap between
sustainability ambitions
and practical integration that produces measurable results can be a challenge.
According to
September 2026 research from Deloitte
, 70% of buyers and suppliers found less than 50% of their sustainability pilots reached multi-site rollout stage.
PepsiCo has signed five letters of intent to explore integrating sustainable startups into its operations. Credit: PepsiCo
“You need to understand how a solution fits into existing operations, whether it can be supported across markets, how it integrates into business processes, and whether the economics support long-term adoption,” Ashley tells Supply Chain Digital.
PepsiCo’s cross-functional approach aims to help startups understand practical requirements early, while giving internal teams opportunities to identify
technical, financial and regulatory barriers
before a wider roll-out.
“Rather than evaluating technologies in isolation, we assessed potential barriers to implementation from multiple business perspectives,” says Ashley.
Utilising PepsiCO’s network of mentors and partners, the IMPACT Edition aims to give startups the ability to consider roadblocks across all stages of the deployment process: from procurement to operations to financing and investments.
“For supply chain leaders, the lesson is simple,” says Ashley. “If you want innovation to scale, you need to involve the people who will ultimately own, operate and support it from the beginning.”
Scaling sustainability initiatives across markets
PepsiCo says it will now assess the possibility of scaling its five selected startups across
its supply chains
“This edition of the PepsiCo Greenhouse Program reflects a deliberate shift from exploring ideas broadly to backing the solutions most capable of creating strategic advantage across the region,” said Anne Tse, CEO of PepsiCo APAC.
Anne Tse, CEO of PepsiCo Asia Pacific. Credit: PepsiCo
This relies on technologies developed in one particular market demonstrating their continued success in different environments.
Geopolitical volatility, differing infrastructure and energy costs differ across territories, while shifting regional regulations present a further challenge. According to the World Economic Forum, 3,000 new trade and industrial policies were introduced globally across 2025 alone.
For PepsiCo, simply replicating a sustainable solution across varying supply chain structures may not always be practical.
“I don't think replication should mean copying and pasting the same solution everywhere,” Ashley says.
“What scales successfully is often not the exact implementation, but the underlying capability the solution provides.”
For supply chain leaders, this means identifying which elements of an innovation can be replicated across markets and which must be adapted to local infrastructure, regulations, supplier capabilities and operational needs.
Collaboration is one way for businesses to market-test and adapt solutions. By working closely with regional teams, suppliers and partners, leaders can gain insights into what pathways need to vary based on local conditions.
“The companies that scale most successfully are usually the ones that balance consistency of ambition with flexibility of execution,” Ashley says.
Beyond emissions: where sustainability meets resilience
For PepsiCo, resilience goals and sustainability initiatives do not need to be separate considerations.
“Sustainability and resilience are increasingly linked,” Ashley says.
“Many of the challenges we face across agriculture, logistics and packaging are also business continuity challenges, whether that is resource availability, climate volatility, operational efficiency or waste management.”
Geopolitical volatility, differing infrastructure and energy costs can make scaling sustainable solutions complex. Credit: PepsiCo
The solutions selected by PepsiCo’s programme can demonstrate how sustainability solutions can have wider business benefits, including contributing to resilience. Takachar’s biochar technology, for example, could create a locally-sourced soil amendment to reduce reliance on external output.
“For me, resilience isn't about predicting every disruption. It's about building supply chains that can adapt when conditions change,” Ashley says.
Key companies
GC Ventures
GC Ventures is the corporate venture capital arm of PTT Global Chemical, bringing expertise in advanced materials, clean technology and biotechnology. Its APAC manufacturing networks can help sustainability startups assess technologies, explore commercial applications and develop pathways towards validation and scale-up. As a partner in PepsiCo’s Greenhouse Program APAC 2026, it supports the programme’s ambition to move promising innovations closer to real-world adoption.
AgFunder Asia
AgFunder Asia is a venture capital investor focused on agrifood technology, with interests spanning artificial intelligence, biology and climate innovation. Through PepsiCo’s Greenhouse Program APAC 2026, it connects participating startups with agrifood technology investors, industry insights and potential strategic partners across the food and agriculture value chain. These connections can help founders explore investment opportunities and commercial pathways as their solutions progress beyond pilots.
Singapore Agri-Food Innovation Lab (SAIL)
The Singapore Agri-Food Innovation Lab (SAIL) is a national platform hosted by Nanyang Technological University Singapore and established in partnership with Enterprise Singapore. It fosters collaboration between corporates, startups, small and medium-sized enterprises and research institutions to advance agri-food innovation. As a PepsiCo Greenhouse Program APAC 2026 partner, SAIL helps connect innovators with research expertise and industry collaborators to explore practical routes towards adoption and growth.

title: Webinar: Keeping on Top of Moving Assets
content:
Webinar: Keeping on Top of Moving Assets
Prioritise Us
on Google
The introduction of RFID has transformed some supply chains, but data availability declines outside RFID enabled environments (Credit: Getty)
An upcoming webinar in partnership with Sensolus on 5 November at 3pm GMT will discuss how companies can retain visibility on cargo across transport modes
As supply chain professionals know, tracking cargo can become challenging after transfers between transport modes.
For organisations managing cargo shipments that travel by truck and then by sea or rail, the visibility of shipment data can be interrupted or cease altogether after multimodal transfers.
In a webinar hosted by
Supply Chain Digital
in partnership with Sensolus, industry experts share insights into how businesses can improve shipment visibility and obtain real-time ETAs without fixed infrastructure or complex IT projects.
Register for the webinar now
to discover how autonomous GPS trackers keep your cargo visible across truck, sea and sea, without fixed infrastructure and complex IT projects.
Moving beyond RFID solutions
The steady rollout of RFID (radio frequency identification) technology has been a significant advance for supply chain professionals.
The IoT based technology has matured in recent years, and has become mainstream infrastructure in some markets.
In April 2026,
switched on RFID sensing across its entire US small package network, enabling every delivery vehicle, every facility, and more than 5,500 The UPS Store locations. The development was backed by more than US$100m dollars of investment.
The results were impressive: misloads fell by nearly 70%, and 20 million manual scans were eliminated - every single day. UPS calls it the most significant visibility advancement in the industry for a decade.
While the introduction of RFID sensors has been a genuine advance, it has only increased the information gap when RFID coverage ceases.
The moment an asset leaves a zone equipped for RFID, whether that's a returnable container heading to a customer site or a trailer sitting in an open yard, there is an interruption in service from the RFID sensor.
In other words, it hasn’t succeeded in closing the visibility gap end to end.
This creates a challenge for organisations who need to know where their assets are at all times, and to understand the condition in which their assets will arrive.
Between 30% and 70% of transit time for multimodal shipments occurs in environments shippers do not own: yards, ports, sidings and vessel holds.
Eliminating visibility blind spots
One of the key hurdles for supply chain managers is the lack of visibility when cargo is transferred between transport modes.
The RFID reading infrastructure of fixed readers, antennas and handheld scanners that enable automatic, real-time tracking of goods are not always present at sea or on board rail logistics. This means other solutions are needed to ensure pallets can be monitored as they move away distribution centres, loading docks and storage areas.
Sensolus’ solution fits right into that gap, bringing location data and status data when other solutions’ signals fade. Its robust battery-powered trackers do not require fixed reader infrastructure, and can supply continuous location and status data for exactly the stretch of the journey where RFID can't see.
Unlike other solutions, Sensolus’ BLE tags are equipped with long-life batteries, ensuring that the information from the tags will continue to arrive long after your cargo has reached its destination.
The production of reliable asset tracking data requires robust trackers and edge intelligence to process the raw data. Credit: Sensolus
Watch the webinar on demand
The webinar includes four speakers from Sensolus:
Kristoff Rattinghe, CEO and Co-Founder
Steven Van Hoof, Vice President, Engineering
Lucas Cardon, Head of Sales Engineers
Pieterjan Blondeel, Head of Marketing
In addition to hearing real life customer experiences, attendees will learn how autonomous trackers can help to provide visibility across every transport leg, modifying their behaviour according to their mode of transport.
They will also learn why complex infrastructure or SIM subscriptions are not necessary to track containers across Europe. Finally, the speakers will explain how the Sensolus platform turns tracker data into reliable ETAs and alerts.
To gain deeper insights into how Sensolus’ solution has helped more than 500 customers across North America and Europe,

title: Stord Expands Fulfilment Capability With AMS Acquisition
content:
Stord Expands Fulfilment Capability With AMS Acquisition
Prioritise Us
on Google
Stord is growing its network with latest AMS acquisition. Credit: Getty
With Stord’s latest acquisition, it is scaling operations and driving greater efficiency across global brands, Stord CEO Sean Henry explains
Ecommerce has undergone significant transformation in recent years, seeing a major increase in demand. Around the world, businesses have a larger market today than ever imagined.
Due to the
rising number of ecommerce platforms
and the ongoing globalisation of trade, fulfilment demands are at an all-time high.
Stord, the physical intelligence layer for independent commerce, has now acquired AMS Fulfillment in order to enhance its own scale and network capabilities.
Growing commerce demands
Stord is a physical intelligence layer for independent commerce, supporting businesses with software, AI and robotics support. Alongside this, it provides access to an efficient and resilient fulfilment network.
The company was founded in 2015 in order to help brands grow their revenue capabilities and better meet customer expectations. It aims to help independent commerce brands gain access to a global market, growing their operations and becoming competitive with larger organisations.
Following a period of growth, having
secured a US$3bn valuation
earlier this year and a US$400m credit facility in October, led by Citi, the company is massively increasing its capabilities. Now, it has announced its largest acquisition to date.
Stord has acquired AMS Fulfillment, a third-party logistics provider. This adds more than 10 million annual orders to its network, covering premium beauty, wellness and high-velocity direct-to-consumer brands.
With the acquisition, Stord gains more than one million square feet across East and West Coast hubs. As a result, its global network is now reaching more than 100 locations, including hubs in Salt Lake City, Philadelphia and Los Angeles.
“Today, I'm proud to announce that Stord has acquired AMS Fulfillment, our largest acquisition to date and our 12th since founding the company,” explains Sean Henry, CEO of Stord on LinkedIn.
Sean Henry, CEO of Stord
At a glance
AMS adds more than 10 million orders to the Stord platform
Through the acquisition, Stord gains nearly 1.3 million square feet of fulfilment infrastructure
Stord’s revenue has grown more than 10x in four years
Stord has raised more than US$300m in funding
Stord reaches one in four US households
Fulfilment investments
Following its US$250m Series F funding in May, Stord launched Stord Labs, a dedicated robotics deployment arm and data foundry. Its capital is going towards global expansion and acceleration of robotics investments.
“At Stord, we're building the infrastructure that enables every brand to deliver Prime-level checkout, delivery and consumer experiences. To do that, scale matters. A lot,” Sean continues.
“More brands bring more volume. More volume drives lower costs, faster delivery speeds and greater efficiency. More facilities put inventory closer to consumers. And every order generates more data to fuel our network intelligence through Stord Labs."
As a network, Stord generates more than eight billion data points every year. With its ongoing growth, it is increasingly supporting high-order-value brands, demonstrating its capabilities in
reliability and speed
, while also maintaining its own personal touch.
With the introduction of AMS to the network, Stord gains access to more than 20 years of commerce experience. Some of its facilities operate autonomously, giving Stord access to new automated capability.
“Premium brands have always understood that fulfilment is part of the product, and AMS was built to honor that,” explains Greg Morello, Chief Executive Officer of AMS Fulfillment.
Greg Morello, Chief Executive Officer of AMS Fulfillment
“Stord shares that conviction and brings the network, intelligence, technology, automation and investment to deliver it at a level few to nobody in the industry can match. Our customers get everything that made AMS great, now backed by the scale and technology to take it further.”
Long-term strategy
Stord aims to make its customers’ supply chain a competitive advantage, offering intelligent orchestration, scale and supply chain optimisation within a single platform. The company is growing rapidly, opening new facilities and expanding its commerce technology in order to remain competitive to ensure its clients can hold their own among the giants.
In the last four years, Stord has grown its revenue more than 10x, with a continuous growth-to-scale transformation.
“Eleven years into building Stord, I believe we're still in the early innings of what this company can become,” Sean adds.
“Brands want the speed and reliability of Prime without sacrificing the personal touches that make them unique. We are building the physical intelligence layer for commerce that makes that possible, and the opportunity ahead of us is massive.”
AMS is Stord’s 12th acquisition and part of its
long-term network expansion strategy
. With ongoing investments and acquisitions, the company is working to build the leading fulfilment network and end-to-end commerce platform. The goal is to gain Prime-like speed and reliability, while also maintaining its own personal approach.
era of expanding commerce
and global trade, Stord is positioning itself as a reliable and efficient contender in the fulfilment industry.
Eleven years into building Stord, I believe we're still in the early innings of what this company can become.
Sean Henry, CEO of Stord
Key companies
CEO:Sean Henry
HQ: Georgia, US
Stord is a supply chain and logistics technology company offering cloud-based warehousing and fulfillment services. Founded in 2015, the platform connects businesses with a network of warehouses and transportation providers, enabling flexible, scalable logistics solutions. Stord serves e-commerce retailers, manufacturers, and enterprises seeking to optimize their supply chain operations through technology-driven infrastructure, providing end-to-end visibility and management capabilities.
AMS Fulfillment
CEO: Greg Morello

title: Amazon: US$18bn To Transform German Logistics Infrastructure
content:
Amazon: US$18bn To Transform German Logistics Infrastructure
Prioritise Us
on Google
Amazon already operates more than 100 sites in Germany and employs more than 40,000 workers. Credit: Amazon
Building on US$112.2bn of prior investment, Amazon will scale physical and digital German infrastructure to enhance supply chains in its biggest EU market
has announced its plans to invest more than US$18bn in Germany through 2027 to strengthen its operations in a critical European hub.
The conglomerate has already invested US$112.2bn in Germany since 2010. Alongside technology upgrades and skills development programmes, the latest commitment will modernise and expand Amazon’s German supply chain infrastructure.
"Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe,” says
David Zapolsky
, Amazon’s Chief Global Affairs and Legal Officer, on LinkedIn.
David Zapolsky, Chief Global Affairs and Legal Officer at Amazon. Credit: Amazon
“Investment at this scale needs the right conditions, including reliable regulatory frameworks, efficient approvals, competitive energy policy and a modern digital administration. We’re encouraged by the direction the Federal Government is taking, and we see ourselves as a long-term partner in getting there.”
Amazon’s investment at a glance:
Amazon plans to invest more than US$18bn in Germany in 2027, covering several business areas.
The programme includes US$5.39bn for AWS cloud and AI infrastructure in the Frankfurt region.
Logistics investment covers new fulfilment capacity and modernisation at existing German sites.
Amazon's German logistics programme includes robotics and other technologies used in fulfilment operations.
The company says its cumulative German investment has exceeded US$112.2bn since 2010.
Modernising logistics and fulfilment infrastructure
While Amazon’s investment programme has a wide span, it carries strong implications for its German fulfilment operations and industrial supply chain.
The company has announced upgrades across six of its German fulfilment centres: Bad Hersfeld, Dortmund and Werne, scheduled for 2027, and Koblenz, Pforzheim and Rheinberg, scheduled for 2028.
New centres in Zweibrucken and Konnern will expand Amazon’s national coverage and generate more than 3,000 jobs.
“We want German businesses, communities, and creators to have the infrastructure and tools they need to compete and grow,” says David.
Alongside physical infrastructure, Amazon is continuing its robotics rollout across its fulfilment network to accelerate work at its German sites. The company will inaugurate a second robotics and AI centre in Berlin, joining its existing R&D base.
“We will keep investing so that German innovation keeps thriving,” says
Stefan Höchbauer,
Vice President of AWS Global Sales for Germany and Central Europe.
Stefan Höchbauer, Vice President of Global Sales for Germany and Central Europe at AWS. Credit: AWS
Amazon’s US$11bn investment scheme in its wider European fulfilment network has already developed
robotic supply chain solutions
. In June 2026 it launched its next-generation
Proteus robot
, designed for manual handling.
The company is also developing Vulcan, designed for product handling. The system has seen early deployment in Germany, at Amazon’s Hamburg facility.
"This transformation is designed to deliver a step-change in how we support our employees and serve our customers," says
Armin Cossmann,
Vice President of Operations for Amazon Europe.
Armin Cossmann, Vice President of Operations for Amazon Europe. Credit: Armin Cossmann via LinkedIn
"Customer expectations aren't slowing down – and neither are we."
AWS’ US$5.39bn German cloud overhaul
As Amazon expands its
physical logistics network
, it plans to support its operations with upgraded digital infrastructure.
AWS plans to commit US$5.39bn – part of the total US$18bn investment – to refining and extending its cloud hub in Frankfurt, Germany’s financial centre. Amazon has also outlined plans for data centre development and will target German AI infrastructure.
For supply chain leaders, AI and cloud infrastructure can support applications across supply planning, inventory management, transport coordination and fulfilment decisions.
September 2026 research from McKinsey demonstrates the increasing prominence of AI and digital platforms in logistics operations: nearly 96% of shippers had adopted AI in warehousing, with 84% reporting a satisfying return on investment.
A further 90% used AI to support transportation, with 88% reporting implementation improved their operations.
“In a fast-moving world, companies need infrastructure they can rely on — secure, available and built to help them stay ahead,” says Stefan.
AWS also counts major German manufacturers and suppliers among its clients, including BMW and Siemens.
Strengthening a strategic market foothold
The investment will build on Amazon’s 25 years in Germany, harnessing an existing web of infrastructure to improve service to a major customer base, as well as neighbouring markets.
"Germany is one of the most important countries in the world for Amazon,” David writes on LinkedIn.
Amazon already operates more than 100 sites in Germany and employs more than 40,000 permanent workers.
It also runs a major innovation centre in Dortmund, where it develops industrial robotics projects for global rollouts. In May 2026, the centre debuted seven new robots to enhance package flow and streamline fulfilment centre operations.
Amazon is developing its second robotics and AI centre in Berlin. Credit: Amazon
Amazon’s FY2025 sales report pinned Germany as its largest European market, with US$46.9bn net sales over the course of the year – a 12.3% increase on the year prior.
Germany is also a central logistics location for Amazon’s European operations. The country possesses strong transport infrastructure and borders nine European countries, including key market France, with links to hubs like Italy and Spain.
“Our job is to keep bringing the infrastructure, technology and local productions that help the whole country compete and grow, and to keep showing up for the long term,” David continues.
Key companies
Siemens is a German technology company specialising in industrial automation, digitalisation, infrastructure and mobility. Since 2023, Siemens Professional Education has worked with AWS’s Skills to Jobs Tech Alliance in Germany to integrate cloud computing into vocational training. The collaboration includes a three-year IT apprenticeship, technical learning programmes and hackathons using AWS cloud and AI services.
DHL is a German international logistics company operating parcel delivery, express shipping, freight forwarding and contract logistics services. Amazon has identified DHL, alongside DPD and Hermes, among its established delivery partners in Germany.
System-Logistik
System-Logistik is a German logistics provider that has worked as an Amazon delivery partner since 2015. The Munich-based company has delivered Amazon parcels in several German cities, including Munich, Mannheim and Frankfurt.

title: Tesla pushes Optimus deliveries to late 2027, says hands still a problem
content:
Tesla Optimus
Fred Lambert
| Oct 22 2026 - 8:56 am PT
Elon Musk now says Tesla will start delivering Optimus humanoid robots to outside customers around the end of 2027. On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call, he said the hands, the robot’s durability and its AI all still need work before then.
Those are the same three problems every humanoid robot company is fighting. And despite Musk’s claim that nobody is close to Tesla, XPeng and Hyundai’s Boston Dynamics look at least as far along.
What Tesla said about Optimus
Musk said Tesla has started early production of Optimus on its high-volume line in Fremont, where Model S and Model X used to be built. Most of a line designed for a million robots a year is installed, but he said it will take at least a year, possibly longer, to reach that rate of about 20,000 units a week, because parts of the design are still changing.
He listed what has to be solved first: the AI, the electromechanical design, and reliability, including making sure the robot doesn’t wear out after a month of use. He expects those issues to be solved around the end of next year. That’s when Tesla expects to deliver Optimus to companies outside Tesla, starting with industrial jobs that are dangerous, repetitive or need to run around the clock.
When an analyst asked where the design was still changing, a Tesla Optimus engineer pointed to the hand as one of the hardest hardware areas, along with custom gears that still carry reliability concerns. Musk agreed the hand is the main issue, explaining that fingers need to be soft enough to handle delicate objects while surviving constant wear, and robots can’t heal like human skin can.
On the AI side, Musk said Tesla is still working through problems with the AI architecture. Tesla doesn’t have a fleet of robots collecting data the way its cars do for FSD, so it plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots and have them practice tasks in what it calls an Optimus Academy. Tesla also plans to put its AI5 chip in Optimus around April 2027.
Musk also promised an Optimus video within a month or two showing the robot doing tasks that aren’t pre-programmed. He argued that many humanoid demos look impressive but only run scripted routines that wouldn’t hold up in the real world.
The same problems we reported last month
None of this is new. Last month, we
reported that Tesla had ramped Optimus to hundreds of units a week
, but that the robots couldn’t generalize to new tasks. According to The Information, the hand and forearm had over 100 small parts assembled by hand, touch sensors had reliability issues, and the AI could take days to learn basic tasks.
Tesla’s own Q3 shareholder letter now calls the bots coming off the Fremont line “the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured.” So every Optimus before this quarter wasn’t production quality.
And the timeline keeps moving. In 2024, Musk said Tesla would build Optimus for internal use in 2025 and hopefully in high volume for other companies in 2026. In January 2025, he said Tesla would build about 10,000 robots that year, with “several thousand” doing useful work by year-end. He later admitted none were. Now external deliveries are a late-2027 target.
Is anyone ahead of Tesla?
Musk said on the call that, to the best of his knowledge, “there is no one that is even close to Tesla” on a general-purpose humanoid robot. That’s hard to square with what competitors have shown.
turned on an automated IRON production line in Guangzhou in September
, with more than 80% of core processes automated. IRON has 21 degrees of freedom in each hand and runs XPeng’s physical AI model on three in-house Turing chips. XPeng plans mass production by the end of 2026, deliveries in the first half of 2027 starting with stores and malls, and a European rollout in the second half of 2027. That’s a similar timeline to Tesla’s, if not slightly ahead.
XPeng is dealing with the same reality. It hasn’t shipped IRON to a paying customer, and its timelines have slipped like everyone else’s.
Boston Dynamics started producing its electric Atlas in January and says all of its 2026 Atlas deployments are already committed, including to Google DeepMind, whose AI models Boston Dynamics is integrating. In September, it opened a robot training center at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia, where Atlas is learning to sequence car parts for the assembly line. Hyundai plans to deploy 25,000 robots across its plants over the next few years. Boston Dynamics also
hired Milan Kovac, Tesla’s former head of Optimus
, in January.
Boston Dynamics also seems to have taken a more pragmatic approach to hands, prioritizing sturdy grippers for industrial parts over human-like dexterity. That’s less impressive in a demo, but it’s a way around the problem Tesla says is holding it back.
Electrek’s Take
Anyone shocked?
Tesla is facing the exact same problems as everyone else: hands that survive real work, robots reliable enough to pay for themselves, and AI that can handle tasks it wasn’t trained for. Nobody has cracked generalization yet, Tesla included. The difference is that Tesla’s competitors aren’t telling investors they have no competition.
Based on what’s public, XPeng has a more automated production line and a similar delivery date, and Boston Dynamics is already deploying Atlas in a car factory with committed customers. Tesla may well have the most robots built, but building robots isn’t the hard part. Making them useful is.
Tesla has promised a video in a month or two. If it shows Optimus doing real, unscripted work, great. But we’ve heard about Optimus timelines before, and they’ve slipped every year. Why should late 2027 be different?

title: New Jersey may finally reverse its draconian e-bike law after massive backlash
content:
New Jersey
Micah Toll
| Oct 22 2026 - 8:02 am PT
New Jersey lawmakers are already looking to walk back one of the country’s most controversial e-bike laws, just months after the sweeping new regulations took effect and sparked widespread backlash from riders, bicycle shops, and advocacy groups.
A newly introduced bill,
, sponsored by State Senator Raj Mukherji, would remove licensing, registration, and insurance requirements for low-speed electric bicycles with motors rated at 750W or less and a maximum motor-powered speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). This includes Class 1 and Class 2 electric bicycles.
The proposal would essentially restore bicycle-like treatment for these two classes of e-bikes, importantly including throttle-equipped models that make up the majority of e-bikes sold in the state and more broadly in the US, while maintaining stricter requirements for faster and more powerful electric bicycles.
The move comes after New Jersey’s previous governor, Phil Murphy,
signed a sweeping e-bike law in January
following several tragic crashes involving young riders.
That legislation, which took full effect in July, eliminated the state’s previous three-class e-bike framework and introduced licensing and registration requirements for all electric bicycles, including ordinary low-speed commuter models. Throttle-equipped and faster e-bikes also faced insurance requirements.
backlash
was intense and immediate.
previously reported
, New Jersey bicycle shops experienced devastating sales declines after the law took effect, with some reporting drops of 20% to 90%. Several businesses were forced to lay off employees, downsize, or even close entirely as e-bike sales and usage plummeted.
Meanwhile, riders faced confusing new requirements that made e-bikes considerably less accessible, which was particularly impactful for lower-income residents, people with disabilities, and those who rely on electric bicycles for daily transportation.
The original law was intended to improve safety, but critics argued that it largely punished responsible riders instead of addressing the growing problem of high-powered electric motorcycles masquerading as bicycles. Only responsible riders actually registered their bikes as required by law, while others were deterred from cycling, and the hooligan riders who often gave e-bikes a bad name continued to ride illegally.
After all, requiring someone riding a 20 mph (32 km/h) commuter e-bike to obtain a driver’s license and register their bicycle does little to address reckless riding on machines capable of highway speeds.
The newly proposed legislation appears to acknowledge that distinction, offering a more targeted approach that could preserve reasonable safety regulations without making ordinary e-bike ownership unnecessarily complicated.
S4830 still needs to work its way through the legislature before becoming law, but for New Jersey’s struggling e-bike industry, it’s a promising sign that lawmakers may finally be listening. It is still widely argued that requiring electric bicycles from 21-28 mph (32-45 km/h) to require a driver’s license and registration is overly burdensome, but at least the state appears to be moving back toward the right direction.

title: Kia's EV6 GT beat out the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7 in a German EV comparison test
content:
Kia EV6 GT
Peter Johnson
| Oct 22 2026 - 7:39 am PT
electric sports car beat out the Tesla Model Y Performance and BYD’s Sealion 7 in a recent comparison test by the German magazine
Auto Motor und Sport
, ranking first overall.
Kia EV6 GT takes first in German performance EV test
It wasn’t a German brand or a Chinese one. It wasn’t even the Tesla Model Y Performance. Kia’s electric sports car, the EV6 GT, took first place in a recent high-performance EV test in Germany, the heart of Europe.
The comparison test, held by German auto magazine
Auto Motor und Sport
, evaluated five high-performance EVs across seven categories: body, safety, comfort and convenience, powertrain, driving performance, environmental friendliness, and running costs.
The EV6 GT ranked first overall with 585 points, 9 points ahead of the Tesla Model Y Performance, which took second with 576 points.
The Zeekr 7GT ranked third with 569 points, followed by the Polestar 4 Coupe Dual Motor with 531 points, and the BYD Sealion 7 AWD Excellence, which ranked fifth with 508 points.
Kia’s electric sports car took the top spot in three of the seven categories: safety, powertrain, and driving performance. In the safety category, the EV6 GT scored highest for its superior braking and high-speed stability.
Kia EV6 GT (Source: Kia Germany)
The EV6 GT earned praise in the powertrain category, boasting up to 650 horsepower and 770 Nm of torque from its dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain.
In the driving performance category, Kia’s electric sports car scored 20 points higher (96 points) than the Tesla Model Y Performance in second (76 points).
According to Auto Motor und Sport, the Kia EV6 GT took first place overall in the comparison test due to its “outstanding driving performance.”
Performance is one thing, but it also stands out with fun features, including Virtual Gear Shift. Borrowed from the Hyundai IONIQ 5 N, the feature simulates the feeling and sounds of a six-speed paddle-operated transmission.
Kia overhauled the interior for the newest model with its new connected car Navigation Cockpit (ccNC) infotainment system.
Kia EV6 GT interior (Source: Kia Germany)
The new system includes dual 12.3″ navigation and driver display screens in a curved panoramic setup.
Kia’s electric sports car can sprint from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds. It uses a new 84 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 279 miles.
With 800V fast-charging capabilities, the Kia EV6 GT can recharge from 10% to 80% in as little as 18 minutes.
In Germany, the
new Kia EV6 GT
starts at 69,990 euros ($78,000). The Tesla Model Y Performance, on the other hand, starts at 63,970 euros in Germany. It offers a WLTP range of up to 360 miles (580 km) and accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in 3.5 seconds.
Which high-performance EV would you drive? The Kia EV6 GT or the Tesla Model Y Performance? Let us know in the comments.
Unfortunately, Kia said it was discontinuing the EV6 GT in the US “until further notice” earlier this year.

title: Fortescue is using KUKA welding robots to handle 6 MW charging cables [video]
content:
EV Charging
Electric Heavy Machinery
Fortescue
Jo Borrás
| Oct 22 2026 - 7:10 am PT
Humanoid robots aren’t ready to juice up the massive, 240-tonne electric haul trucks Fortescue is putting to work in Australia’s punishing Pilbara. Instead, the company is using specially modified and massively powerful automotive assembly-line robots from KUKA to wrangle the massive cables needed to deliver a mind-bending 6 MW of power to its trucks’ batteries.
While Chinese car brands capable of 2 MW “
flash charging
” are making headlines these days,
Fortescue and Liebherr have been quietly working together to develop a 6MW charging system for their massive
, ultra heavy-duty mining rigs since 2024 – but details about how the process actually works have been scarce.
Until now, that is. In a new video released by the company earlier this month, Fortescue explains how it delivers what amounts a controlled lightning bolt into the battery of its specially developed, 264 (short)
ton Liebherr T264E electric haul truck
. And, because the massive, liquid-cooled copper cables are too big, too heavy, and too dangerous for any human to handle, of course they’re using robots to get the job done.
“The challenge with a six megawatt charger is that nobody makes these, and therefore nobody makes a lot of the components, either,” says a Fortescue representative, in the video. “So, we’ve had to take systems and subsystems from different industries were using industrial robots that would normally be used for welding in a car factory.”
A little help, please
KUKA robot charger; via Fortescue.
Fortescue was able to develop and refine its KUKA robots with help from a $10 million (AUD) grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), which were earmarked to help the company develop a six megawatt (MW)
fast charger test unit and support its ultimate goal of achieving true net zero operations by 2030
“Leveraging our world-class capability in battery and charging solutions from motorsport, the fast chargers have been developed for the challenging conditions of the Pilbara,”
explained Fortescue Zero’s then-Chief Executive Officer, Ellie Coates
, when the grant was announced in 2024. “Equipped with robotic connection options, they will be able to power Fortescue’s future 240-tonne Liebherr T 264 battery electric trucks in just 30 minutes.”
The Liebherr T264E packs an impossibly large 3.2 MWh (3,200 kWh) battery pack – the equivalent capacity of about 40 road-going Tesla Model Y crossovers – to put that 30 minute spec into context.
