title: Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B
content:
Fred Lambert
| Oct 22 2026 - 7:00 am PT
Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.
The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.
Tesla’s 2026 capex guidance keeps moving
Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”
Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”
Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.
The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”
There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.
Where Tesla’s Q3 free cash flow came from
Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:
Net income
Depreciation, amortization and impairment
Stock-based compensation
Other non-cash items (FX, taxes, bitcoin, SpaceX)
Changes in working capital
Operating cash flow
Capital expenditures
Free cash flow
Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.
The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.
Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.
Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.
Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.
If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.
Tesla’s borrowing plans
The capex cut comes a month after Tesla
signed $30 billion of new credit facilities
. The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.
Electrek’s Take
None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from
Wednesday’s results
says less about the business than it seems.
Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.
The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

title: The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E gains a standard long-range battery and starts at $40,000
content:
Ford Mustang Mach E
Peter Johnson
| Oct 22 2026 - 6:00 am PT
Ford opened orders for the 2027
Mustang Mach-E
, which now offers a standard extended-range battery for under $40,000. A new Trail model is also joining the lineup.
2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E prices and range
Ford’s electric crossover SUV is back for another model year. The 2027 Mustang Mach-E drops the standard-range battery offered in the 2026 model and now comes standard with the larger 88 kWh battery.
The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-e is available in five trims: Select, Premium, GT, Rally, and a new purpose-built Trail model.
The new 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail is available for a $2,295 package upgrade for the Select eAWD.
According to Ford, the new Trail package is designed to make “outdoor adventures across pavement, gravel, and dirt roads more accessible than ever.”
It features fine-tuned front and rear struts and springs, a Rally-shaped steering rack, 19-inch High Gloss Dark Carbonized Gray Wheels with as-cast graphics, and is 10 mm taller in the front and 15 mm taller in the rear than the base Mach-E.
2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail (Source: Ford)
The 2027 Mustang Mach-E Trail comes with standard 400W, 120V Pro Power Onboard. It’s available as an upgrade for other variants, including the Premium, GT, and Mustang Mach-E Rally.
Select and Premium models use the 88 kWh battery and are available with rear- or all-wheel-drive (eAWD) powertrains. The GT and Rally variants use the 91 kWh battery and are only sold as eAWD models.
2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail (Source: Ford)
Ford’s BlueCruise 1.5 comes standard on the GT and Rally and optional on Select with Tech Pack Lite and Premium with Premium Tech Pack models. The Trail requires the hardware selection at the time of ordering. It cannot be added later.
Meanwhile, the Ford Connectivity Package and Ford Security Package are standard across the entire 2027 lineup.
2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail interior (Source: Ford)
The base 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Select RWD starts at $39,995. Including the $2,045 destination fee, prices start at $42,040.
While it is a bit more expensive than the 2026 model year, Ford no longer offers the standard-range battery. Ford said a new secondary front motor delivers the same performance as the previous unit but at a lower cost, enabling the lower-priced base RWD model with the extended-range battery.

title: Redwood and Rivian set to expand their EV battery recycling partnership
content:
EV batteries
Redwood Materials
JB Straubel
Jo Borrás
| Oct 22 2026 - 4:00 am PT
Redwood Materials and Rivian are expanding their existing EV battery partnership, adding a fresh battery material recycling effort to the EV startup’s Normal, Illinois, vehicle factory and, potentially, other Rivian-owned sites.
As Tesla co-founder JB Straubel’s second act, Redwood Materials had a lot to live up to. Its plan to give used EV batteries a second life as energy storage for public- and private-sector buildings, construction sites, micro-grids, and (sigh) data centers makes plenty of sense, though. Enough sense, anyway, that Rivian decided to put the idea to work as it built out its R2 production line at the former Diamond-Star Mitsubishi plant in Normal.
Back in April
the upstart EV brand signed on for 10 MWh worth of energy storage using repurposed Rivian battery packs
– but that deal was just the beginning.
The new, expanded partnership between the two companies will see Redwood collect, sort, and recycle Rivian’s battery production scrap materials, putting them safely back into the manufacturing process with minimal waste and at a fraction of the cost of virgin material. What’s more, the new deal will see retired Rivian batteries put to use in other stationary energy projects before eventually recycling some 99% of those batteries’ critical materials (nickel, cobalt, copper, and lithium).
With the recent launch of what is sure to be the more popular
, more affordable R2, that’s suddenly a much bigger deal than it might have been last year.
Bigger markets, bigger deals
2027 R2; via Rivian.
“Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials,” explains Straubel. “Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible, and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keep rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”
Rivian is the latest major EV brand to enter into a formal battery recycling partnership with Redwood, with the list of others including BMW, Ford, Toyota, and Volvo.

title: PVH expands Houston footprint to scale pre-assembled solar trackers - pv magazine Global
content: Solar tracker and foundation solution provider PV Hardware USA (PVH USA) has announced a major expansion of its original Houston, Texas, manufacturing facility. The expansion adds approximately 3,180 m2 of manufacturing space, increasing the company’s overall Houston footprint capacity by 42%. The company said the added space will support a 35% increase in the production of pre-assembled tracker components. The move is designed to shift complex component assembly away from outdoor construction jobsites and into a controlled factory environment. “We are investing in additional domestic manufacturing capacity because our customers are asking us to do more,” said Alfonso Queipo, CEO of PVH USA. “Pre-assembly has become an important part of that strategy because it allows us to move complexity out of the field and into an environment where we have greater control over quality, productivity and consistency.” The project builds upon PVH USA’s growing footprint in Texas. In May 2024, the company invested $30 million to launch its first Houston facility, followed by the addition of a 95,000-square-foot tracker factory in September 2025. Factory precision vs. field complexity Since 2023, PVH USA has focused on refining its pre-assembly model to streamline utility-scale installations and offset field labor shortages facing EPCs and developers. According to the company, completing sub-assembly tasks in the factory before equipment is shipped to project sites offers significant operational advantages. This approach reduces the number of loose components delivered on-site by up to 70%, with approximately 188 loose parts per row assembled in the factory rather than in the field. As a result, field installation rates can improve by up to 44%. By shifting assembly work to a controlled factory environment, the company also reduces on-site labor requirements, improves project scheduling predictability, and minimizes workers’ exposure to adverse weather conditions, particularly during severe weather events or under tight project deadlines. “Solar EPCs face mounting pressure regarding labor availability, strict timelines and total project costs,” said Rodolfo Bitar, vice president of business development for PVH USA. “Traditionally, manufacturers pushed the assembly burden onto the jobsite. We ask a different question: what work can be done more efficiently before the equipment ever leaves the factory?” Domestic content and sustainability In addition to site efficiency gains, PVH USA highlighted the sustainability and supply chain benefits of expanding domestic production in Texas. Localizing sub-assembly reduces the carbon emissions associated with long-haul international shipping while increasing domestic content compliance under U.S. clean energy incentive frameworks. The company noted that steel accounts for more than 98% of the total weight of a PVH solar tracker system, enabling high end-of-life recyclability. The expansion complements PVH’s existing terrain- and weather-resilient product portfolio, including its terrain-following AxoneDuo Infinity tracker (which accommodates up to 2 degrees of post-to-post slope variation) and its HazardPVH extreme weather mitigation software suite. title: TCL Sunpower launches hybrid energy storage cabinet for C&I applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Chinese manufacturer has unveiled a 100 kWh scalable energy storage cabinet for the European market. The company plans to bring a full portfolio of commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage to the continent soon.
Matthew Lynas
22 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
TCL SunPower has launched a new hybrid energy storage cabinet for the commercial and industrial (C&I) segment in Europe.
The X5 has a base unit rated at 50 kW/100 kWh and scaled to 400 kWh by connecting up to four units in parallel. TCL SunPower’s new C&I cabinet integrates a 50 kW inverter and is delivered as a factory-assembled, pre-wired solution, which the manufacturer claims can reduce installation costs by up to 60% compared with systems assembled on site.
The cabinet is 1.9 m tall, has a 1.37 m
footprint and weighs 1,200 kg. The X5 is rated IP66 for the inverter and IP 55 for the cabinet and operates at temperatures from – 60 C to 50 C.
TCL SunPower is marketing the X5 as a compact unit built for sites that are too small to justify a custom engineered battery system, but too demanding for a residential product. The X5 can accommodate on-grid, off-grid and microgrid operation with product specifications recording islanding in less than 20 milliseconds and black-start capability without any grid or PV connection. The system accepts generator input up to 138 kVA.
Integrated safety features and system management features include three layers of monitoring across cabinet, battery pack, while individual cells support fire suppression, gas detection and arc-fault interruption. They system is managed through TCL’s energy management controller and a web or app interface. TCL SunPower described the cabinet as “VPP ready” and noted compliance with GDPR European data protection regulation and ETSI EN303645 cybersecurity requirements.
Steven Zhang, general manager at TCL SunPower Global described the X5 as a “first milestone” in a broader strategy that will see the manufacturer bring a full C&I storage portfolio to Europe.
“Over the next 12 months, we will expand from hybrid storage systems for small and medium businesses to megawatt-scale solutions, allowing our partners to address a much wider range of customer needs. We enter this market with a strong industrial foundation already in place.”
TCL SunPower’s X5 cabinet has already been deployed at some sites in Europe, including at Spain, where installer Electricidad EUFON has used a TCL X5 to convert an existing off-grid solar water-pumping system first installed in 2015 without battery storage into a hybrid system without expanding the site’s solar array.

title: Sonnen files for insolvency - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
German battery storage manufacturer Sonnen has filed for insolvency, months after Shell sold the company to family office Tiven. The company plans to continue serving its 150,000-plus customers while restructuring or liquidating several subsidiaries.
Sandra Enkhardt
22 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Sonnen headquarters in Allgäu, Germany.
This summer, after years of searching for a buyer, oil major Shell sold German battery storage manufacturer Sonnen to family office Tiven. The company, based in Wildpoldsried in Germany’s Allgäu region, has now filed for insolvency, according to German business daily
Handelsblatt
The newspaper reported that Sonnen GmbH’s approximately 400 remaining employees were informed of the insolvency filing on Thursday morning. Although no official notice has yet been published in the insolvency register, the company confirmed the proceedings to
Handelsblatt
According to the report, Sonnen will continue serving its existing customer base of more than 150,000 clients. However, numerous subsidiaries are expected to be liquidated or placed into insolvency proceedings under self-administration.
Handelsblatt
reported that only one production facility will remain operational.
Sonnen did not respond to a request for comment from
pv magazine
. “We remain in Spain and have high expectations here,” Franc Comino, managing director of Sonnen Ibérica, told
pv magazine
In late August. However, the company did not respond to subsequent inquiries.
pv magazine
‘s reporting following Tiven’s acquisition of Sonnen had already raised questions about the company’s future this summer. The communications agency representing Sonnen in Germany also declined to comment on the company’s business strategy following the takeover.
On the same day, Sonnen USA reported strong growth and confirmed the acquisition of its entire global business by Tiven. The US subsidiary said its sales in the United States had doubled year-on-year, while production had tripled. The company had also expanded its manufacturing facility in the US state of Georgia, partly to reduce its dependence on global supply chains.
The company said it currently expects to sell more than 180 MWh of residential battery storage capacity in the United States this year. The main drivers of this growth are its virtual power plant (VPP) activities, particularly its partnership with Solrite. According to the company, more than 6,000 households in Texas alone are already participating in the model, which combines solar installations, battery storage, energy management and integration into virtual power plants.
“Sonnen USA remains firmly focused on innovation in virtual power plants and further growth in the United States,” said CEO Blake Richetta. “Tiven is fully committed to the long-term success of Sonnen USA and supports the company in its ambition to become a leading player in the North American virtual power plant market.”
The company declined to comment on developments at Sonnen in Germany when contacted by
pv magazine

title: Aiko to convert PERC factory into 6 GW of ABC cell capacity - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Chinese company says it will convert the manufacturing capacity at its base in Tianjin into its proprietary all-back-contact (ABC) technology as the efficiency of passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) solar cells reaches “a bottleneck”.
Patrick Jowett
22 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Highlights
Aiko’s G4 Infinite Ultra ABC solar module
Chinese solar cell and module maker
Aiko Solar
has revealed plans to upgrade and convert its Tianjin base from passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) solar cell capacity to 6 GW of its all-back-contact (ABC) cell capacity.
Aiko’s proprietary ABC cells feature n-type technology which shifts all electrical grid lines and busbars from the front surface to the rear side of the cell. The architecture is intended to increase light absorption and improve aesthetics, particularly for rooftop and distributed PV applications.
A filing on the Shanghai Stock Exchange explains that project will utilise the existing PERC plant as the production workshop, adding new process production equipment and upgrading supporting power auxiliary equipment and facilities.
“This capacity upgrade will introduce the company’s latest ABC technology, producing ABC battery products with higher conversion efficiency, better product performance, and greater market competitiveness,” the filing adds.
Aiko estimates total investment for the project will reach CNY 1.15 billion ($172.2 million), of which CNY 1.131 billion is for fixed assets and CNY 19 million is for initial and working capital. It will be raised through various means, the company says, including own capital, financing from financial institutions and cooperation with industry ecosystem partners.
In the filing, Aiko’s Board of Directors explains the upgrade aligns with the development trend of the photovoltaic industry and is consistent with the company’s strategic development direction. They add that current p-type PERC cell mass production efficiency has “reached a bottleneck”, with market demand declining, prices falling and cells facing the risk of rapid obsolescence.
“After this technological upgrade, related production capacity will be fully upgraded to ABC technology, offering higher photoelectric conversion efficiency, better aesthetics and improved safety,” the directors add.
The upgrade is planned to start in the fourth quarter of this year, before gradually entering production in the third quarter of 2027.
Aiko introduced its
fourth-generation G4 Infinite Ultra module
in July, extending its ABC module platform into the 690 W power class.

title: Iraq removes import tariffs on solar systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The measure coincides with the completion of a draft set of regulations set to govern the connection of solar energy systems to Iraq’s national grid.
Patrick Jowett
22 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Manufacturing
The government of Iraq has decided to eliminate customs duties on solar energy systems imported into the country.
According to reports from the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the country’s Council of Ministers decided on the measure “to support the transition toward renewable energy sources and reduce the costs associated with acquiring such systems”.
The removal of customs duties follows a formal proposal submitted by Iraq’s Electricity Minister, Ali Saadi Waheeb, to the Prime Minister last month, which requested a reduction in customs duties on solar energy systems.
The rate was originally as high as 33% but was
reduced to 5%
in February this year with the reduction covering PV panels, cables, inverters and lithium batteries. It followed a move by Iraq’s Central Bank earlier in the month to grant loans worth IQD 6 billion ($4.6 million) for solar energy systems.
INA’s latest update adds that the Ministry of Electricity has completed a draft set of regulations that will govern the connection of solar systems to Iraq’s national grid.
The news agency explained the regulations, comprising 40 articles, are designed to “establish mechanisms for grid interconnection and the exchange of electrical energy between citizens and the national network.” They will also permit citizens to connect their solar systems to the national grid by using smart meters.
The ministry says it has reached out to Iraq’s State Council to finalise the legal drafting of the regulations. It will then be submitted to the country’s Council of Ministers for formal approval.
Iraq’s solar market is gaining momentum, with its
first solar module production line
, located in the Karbala governorate of central Iraq, reaching inauguration in July.
A 300 MW solar project is currently under development in Karbala, with the
first phase
, totaling 22 MW, going live in September 2025. The country’s largest solar project under development, a planned 1 GW in the southeastern governorate of Basra,
entered trial operation
in March with the switching on of 61 MW.

title: Rwanda tenders 200 MW floating PV, 800 MWh BESS project - pv magazine Global
content:

A tender is open in Rwanda for a 200 MW floating solar plant to be tied to 800 MWh of battery storage. The deadline to submit pre-qualification bids is November 12.
Patrick Jowett
22 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Rwanda’s Energy Development Corporation Limited (EDCL) has opened a tender for a 200 MW floating solar power plant alongside an 800 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS). The project is set to be built at Lake Sake, within the Ngoma district of Rwanda’s Eastern province.
Available tender details
explain the project will be structured as an independent power producer scheme, with the chosen developer set to enter a long-term power purchase agreement with the state-owned Rwanda Energy Group (REG) through its subsidiary, the Energy Utility Corporation Limited (EUCL), which will act as the offtaker.
The selected bidder will be responsible for the design, supply, installation, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of the floating PV system and BESS. Interested bidders are required to have at least 10 years experience in designing, constructing and managing renewable energy power plants.
The tender kicks off with a pre-qualification round, with interested independent power producers expected to meet a series of administrative, technical and financial requirements as set out in pre-qualification documents available on REG’s website.
A site visit for potential applicants is taking place on October 23. The deadline to submit initial bids, which must be sent electronically, is November 12.
Rwanda’s solar market is still in its relative infancy. The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has tracked 47.5 MW of operational solar across the country to date, according to figures available in the association’s project database.
There are relatively few operational floating PV plants across Africa despite research identifying significant potential in deploying solar on the continent’s inland bodies of water. A
2023 study
found Africa could generate 100 GW of solar by installing on 1% of its 100,000 sqm of reservoirs.
The largest floating solar project under development in Africa is a
project on Lake Kariba, the world’s largest artificial lake and reservoir by volume, on Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. Last December, government officials in Zimbabwe said work would begin on the site this year, beginning with an initial 150 MW phase.
The largest operational floating PV project in Africa to date is a
13 MW array
in Morocco, which came online in July.

title: Engie starts building first co-located solar and battery project in France - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Engie has begun construction of its first co-located solar and battery project in France, combining 29.8 MW of solar capacity with a 20 MWh battery system to shift electricity delivery to periods of higher grid demand.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
22 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
French energy company Engie has started construction of a 29.8 MW solar plant paired with a 20 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Saint-Jean-Froidmentel, in France’s Centre-Val de Loire region. The project, known as Parc du Buisson, is the company’s first co-located solar and storage development in France.
The plant is being built on a former quarry site spanning 23 hectares and will feature nearly 46,000 solar panels. The battery system will have a power output of 8.8 MW, allowing it to discharge for more than two hours at full power.
The batteries will store some of the electricity generated when solar production is abundant and release it when grid demand is higher. This will shift the timing of electricity delivery, add flexibility to the power system and help align solar generation with periods when it is more useful to the grid.
Engie says it has 10.7 GW of energy storage capacity in operation and under construction worldwide.
The solar plant and battery system will share the same site and an approximately 11 km grid connection to a substation. According to Engie, this approach reduces the number of grid connection requests, lowers associated costs and improves the economics of both installations.
Construction began in September 2026 with earthworks and access roads. The next stages include foundations, installation of mounting structures and solar modules, and deployment of battery containers and electrical equipment.
Grid connection is scheduled for summer 2027, with the entire project expected to enter operation in December 2027.
The project is expected to generate €122,000 ($137,000) in annual tax revenue for local authorities. The municipality will also receive nearly €90,000 through Engie’s “Bon Énergie” scheme.

title: Solar-assisted CO₂ heat pump achieves 18.7% COP increase as irradiance rises - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Italy have tested a 10 kW dual-source heat pump using CO₂ as a refrigerant and air or photovoltaic-thermal collectors as heat sources. The results show that solar operation can improve heating performance under favorable irradiance conditions, while an optimized source-switching strategy delivers modest annual electricity savings.
Lior Kahana
22 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Heat pumps
Residential
The experimental setup
A research team in Italy has investigated the performance of a direct-expansion, dual-source heat pump that uses air and solar energy as heat sources and CO₂ as the refrigerant. The researchers aimed to identify optimal operating conditions and develop advanced control strategies.
“An experimental campaign was carried out under real-field conditions on a 10 kW prototype, considering both Air-Mode and Sun-Mode operation for domestic hot water production and producing a total of 307 tests,” the researchers said. “To overcome the limitations of non-uniform experimental data, artificial neural networks (ANNs) were developed to predict system performance over a wider operating domain.”
The researchers installed the 10 kW heat pump at a research center in Rome, Italy. The prototype operated either with a fan-assisted air evaporator or with CO₂ flowing through copper tubes attached to the rear of 10 photovoltaic-thermal (PVT) collectors. The collectors were south-facing and installed at a tilt angle of 48 degrees.
An additional water circuit, equipped with a 300-liter storage tank, simulated domestic hot water production. The researchers maintained the water inlet temperature at 20 C and adjusted the flow rate to achieve an outlet temperature of approximately 60 C.
During testing, the team varied the compressor frequency from 50 Hz to 70 Hz and monitored refrigerant temperatures, pressures and mass flow rates, along with solar irradiance and total heat pump electricity consumption. Measurements were recorded every 0.5 seconds and averaged over five-second intervals.
The resulting dataset comprised 164 test points in air mode and 143 in solar mode. The researchers used the data to calculate heating capacity and coefficient of performance (COP).
The results showed that solar operation offered a thermodynamic advantage under favorable irradiance conditions. As solar irradiance increased from 322 W/m² to 904 W/m², the refrigerant evaporation temperature rose from 4 C to 12.9 C, reducing the required compression work.
Heating capacity increased by 21.1%, from 8.75 kW to 10.6 kW, while COP improved by 18.7%.
“Conversely, under low irradiance conditions, Air-Mode remained more efficient due to the lower thermal resistance of the air evaporator,” the researchers said. “These results confirm the existence of a minimum irradiance threshold above which Sun-Mode becomes advantageous.”
The team also trained artificial neural networks to predict electricity consumption, COP and compressor frequency in both operating modes. The researchers compared system performance at heating capacities of 8.5 kW and 10 kW and water temperatures ranging from 20 C to 60 C to identify optimal conditions for switching between air and solar operation.
They then conducted annual simulations for seven locations – Rome, Tenerife, San Diego, Toronto, Mexico City, Perth and Beijing – using five domestic hot water demand profiles and a 900-liter storage tank.
“The results show that, although the electrical energy savings associated with the source-switching strategy remain limited (approximately 100–120 kWh/year under the most favorable conditions), the simultaneous electricity generation of the PV/T field significantly affects the overall economic performance of the system,” the researchers said.
The techno-economic assessment also revealed substantial differences between locations. Simple payback periods ranged from approximately six to 10 years in areas with high solar availability to more than 20 years in less favorable climates.
“A complementary thermo-economic assessment highlighted a strong dependence on climatic conditions, with simple payback periods ranging from approximately 6–10 years in locations characterized by high solar availability to over 20 years in less favorable climates,” the researchers added.
The findings are presented in “
CO₂ dual-source (air/solar) heat pump on-field testing: results and performance maps development for optimal mode selection
,” published in
Applied Thermal Engineering
. The research team included scientists from Italy’s
University of Naples Federico II
Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (ENEA)

title: Spanish region announce tax on ground mounted PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Spanish region of Castilla y León plans to extend its environmental impact tax to ground-mounted solar installations from 2027. Spanish solar association UNEF has criticised the proposal, arguing that PV projects already face multiple taxes and that the new levy lacks environmental justification.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
22 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
The Spanish region of Castilla y León plans to extend its environmental impact tax to large-scale photovoltaic installations from 2027 under a draft bill on tax, financial and administrative measures.
The proposed reform would expand the scope of a tax currently applied to wind farms, hydroelectric reservoirs and high-voltage power lines. Fixed telecommunications networks would also become subject to the levy.
According to the draft legislation, the changes are intended to reflect the evolution of economic activities in the region and ensure greater neutrality and fairness in the taxation of activities with similar economic objectives and potential environmental impacts.
The bill identifies solar farms as installations that can affect landscapes, flora and fauna, occupy land and alter traditional land uses.
The regional government justifies the proposed tax by invoking the European Union’s “polluter pays” principle. It also notes that Castilla y León is a net exporter of renewable electricity, meaning that local communities bear some of the environmental impacts associated with electricity generation for consumption elsewhere.
Under the proposal, solar farms would be taxed according to the surface area they occupy. The tax liability would remain in place even after a facility ceases operating, until it has been fully dismantled and the site restored to its original condition.
The draft legislation also sets out exemption criteria for certain self-consumption installations. Ground-mounted self-consumption systems occupying 5 hectares or more would qualify for an exemption only if the ratio of contracted power capacity during the P1 peak tariff period to installed generation capacity is at least 50%.
If this threshold is not met, the authorities could determine that the installation’s primary purpose is to sell electricity to the grid, making it subject to the tax. Rooftop PV installations and ground-mounted systems occupying less than 5 hectares would be exempt.
José Donoso, director general of Spanish solar association UNEF, described the proposed tax as “purely a revenue-raising measure and entirely unjustified,” arguing that solar installations already generate substantial tax revenue at national and local levels.
UNEF said PV projects are subject to several taxes, including the tax on economic activities (IAE), the tax on the value of electricity production (IVPEE) and the special electricity tax (IEE), as well as municipal levies such as the construction, installations and works tax (ICIO) and property tax (IBI-BICES).
According to the association, municipalities hosting solar farms receive approximately €10,000 ($11,232) per installed MW annually in tax revenue.
UNEF also questioned the environmental justification for the levy, arguing that solar projects must already undergo environmental impact assessments before receiving approval from the relevant authorities. The association said imposing an additional tax on projects that have obtained favourable environmental assessments is unjustified.
UNEF also raised concerns about how the revenue would be used. It argued that if the tax is intended to address the environmental and territorial impacts of solar installations, the proceeds should benefit the communities hosting the projects. However, according to the association, the draft legislation provides for the revenue to be incorporated into Castilla y León’s general budget rather than earmarked for affected municipalities.
UNEF also criticised the proposal to calculate the tax according to the number of hectares occupied rather than the electricity generated. The association argued that a land-based levy would fail to account for differences in electricity production between solar installations across Castilla y León.
Two solar farms occupying the same area could generate different amounts of electricity because of variations in solar irradiation, equipment efficiency and project design, but would face the same tax liability based on their land footprint, UNEF said.
If approved, Castilla y León would become Spain’s third autonomous community to introduce a specific tax on PV installations, following Aragón and La Rioja. UNEF claimed that the proposed levy would be higher than those already imposed in the other two regions.

title: Rio Tinto plans 360 MWh thermal battery for Australian alumina refinery - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Rio Tinto is assessing a 360 MWh thermal battery to replace fossil fuels in alumina refining, with the proposed Australian project potentially cutting annual emissions by 67,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide.
David Carroll
22 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Mining giant Rio Tinto and thermal energy storage specialist
Rondo Energy
have commenced front-end engineering and design on a project seeking to integrate a 30 MW/360 MWh heat battery into the existing steam system at the Yarwun alumina refinery near Gladstone.
The companies said if delivered, the project would be one of the first large-scale demonstrations of thermal energy storage for industrial process heat globally, and a world-first for the alumina industry.
Kira Rundel, head of Rondo in Australia, said the project will help validate the role of thermal energy storage in reducing fossil fuel use in energy-intensive industries and pave the way for similar projects in other sectors.
“This project shows how Australia’s abundant energy can become a competitive advantage for industry,” she said. “Heat batteries allow manufacturers to use low-cost electricity to produce the reliable, round-the-clock heat their operations need.”
The project, supported by a grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), will seek to integrate a 30 MW / 360 MWh thermal energy storage unit into the Yarwun refinery’s existing steam system.
Rondo said its heat batteries, built on proven refractory brick materials as the thermal storage medium, can store low-cost grid electricity generated during sunny and windy hours as high-temperature heat for days and release it when needed to generate steam for industrial operations. The company said the heat is typically delivered as steam or hot air up to 1,000°C and the technology has a round-trip efficiency of more than 98%.
California-headquartered Rondo said for energy-intensive industries such as alumina refining, the heat batteries offer a fast, low-cost pathway to electrification that addresses both emissions and energy costs.
“Because the heat battery slots into the existing steam network, the facility’s processes run exactly as before, the only thing that changes is the energy for that heat: no longer from fossil fuels, but sourced from low-cost electricity instead,” the company said.
The Yarwun study will assess the technical and economic viability of integrating the technology into the refinery operations.
Alumina refining is a notoriously hard-to-abate industry and Rio Tinto Pacific Operations Managing Director Armando Torres said industrial process heat remains one of the toughest
decarbonization
challenges.
“Reducing emissions from alumina refining is complex, particularly when it comes to generating the high-pressure steam needed for our operations,” he said.
“This study will help us determine whether thermal energy storage can provide a technically and economically viable alternative to fossil fuels for part of Yarwun’s steam requirements.”
If the Yarwun project is progressed, it is expected to cut onsite emissions by about 67,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide each year.
ARENA’s funding for the project will be delivered in two phases, with an initial AUD 3.6 million ($2.5 million) to complete front-end engineering and design work, followed by up to AUD 38 million for full-scale construction and commissioning should the project proceed, as well as up to AUD 33.3 million in conditional contingency support.
ARENA Chief Executive Officer Darren Miller said technologies such as
thermal energy storage
need to be tested in real large-scale operating environments before they can be adopted more broadly across Australian industry.
“This project will test whether thermal energy storage can provide a practical pathway to lower emissions from industrial heat in a real-world operating environment, where reliability, performance and integration are critical,” he said. “Demonstrations like this will help build the evidence industry needs to make future investment decisions so the value of this project extends well beyond a single refinery.”

title: Robots get 15% better trajectory tracking for flying and walking with new framework
content: Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have developed a learning method that helps robots improve task performance while maintaining stability. The approach combines reinforcement learning with control theory to provide stability guarantees and improve tracking performance by up to 15 percent compared with existing methods. The method, called contraction-aware reinforcement learning, is designed for robots with different forms of movement, including wheeled, flying, and six-legged platforms. The researchers said the approach could make deploying learning-based robotic systems more practical by reducing the risk of instability and costly damage during operation. Robots learn stability The reinforcement learning method helps robots follow desired paths while maintaining stability. Called Contraction-Aware Reinforcement Learning (CARL), the technique combines reinforcement learning with contraction theory to improve control performance and provide mathematical guarantees on how tracking errors behave. The researchers tested the method on three different robotic platforms: a wheeled TurboBot 3 Burger, a flapping aerial drone, and a six-legged Jethexa robot. The experiments showed that CARL improved tracking performance by up to 15 percent compared with existing methods, including during tests on physical robots. Reinforcement learning allows robots to develop control strategies through repeated interactions with their environments. The system learns from feedback, adjusting its actions to improve performance and achieve a target objective. However, reinforcement learning does not inherently guarantee that a robot will remain stable while executing a learned policy. A robot may learn an effective way to complete a task but still exhibit unpredictable behavior or deviate excessively from its intended trajectory. CARL addresses this challenge by integrating reinforcement learning with contraction theory, a mathematical framework used to analyze the stability of dynamic systems. The approach allows reinforcement learning to serve as the robot’s main controller while providing limits on how much tracking errors can grow. According to the research team, small tracking errors may still occur, but the method establishes mathematical bounds on their magnitude. This provides a way to combine the adaptability of learning-based control with the stability requirements of physical robotic systems. The approach aims to help robots achieve their objectives without allowing deviations from their intended behavior to become excessive. Learning reliable movement The researchers first evaluated CARL in computer simulations before moving to physical experiments in an aerospace engineering flight laboratory. They tested the technique on three robots with different movement mechanisms: a wheeled TurboBot 3 Burger, a flapping aerial drone, and a six-legged Jethexa robot. This allowed the team to examine how the control method performed across different types of robotic dynamics. A major challenge in transferring learned control strategies from simulations to physical machines is the sim-to-real gap. A robot’s actual physical properties may differ from the values used to train its controller in a simulated environment. For example, a simulation may represent a robot as weighing 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds), while the real machine weighs 1.2 kilograms (2.6 pounds). Such discrepancies can affect how a robot responds to control commands and follows a planned trajectory. The researchers reported that CARL handled these uncertainties more effectively than existing methods. Its improved tracking performance was observed not only in simulations but also during real-world testing, suggesting that the technique can maintain its advantages beyond computer-generated environments. The researchers identified wildfire management as one possible application for the technology. Robots deployed in hazardous environments could help locate hotspots, gather information, or deliver supplies to first responders. In such situations, reliable movement and predictable control are important because unexpected deviations could compromise a robot’s ability to complete its assigned task. The researchers have made the method openly available, with implementation code published on GitHub.

title: 30% less fuel: US Air Force funds Natilus' KONA cargo aircraft
content: The US Air Force has awarded aerospace manufacturer Natilus $3.5 million to advance its KONA regional cargo aircraft toward full-scale flight testing and a military logistics demonstration. The optionally piloted aircraft is designed to carry 3.8 tons of cargo while using less fuel than comparable conventional aircraft.The funding comes from Operational Energy – Innovation and the Department of the Air Force through the Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Energy, Installations, and Environment. It will support development of KONA as a potential option for moving supplies across dispersed military operating locations, including in fuel-constrained environments.Natilus is developing KONA around a blended-wing-body configuration, in which the aircraft’s body and wings form a more integrated shape than those of a conventional tube-and-wing aircraft. The company said the design consumes approximately 30 percent less fuel than comparable conventional aircraft.Support regional military airliftKONA is intended to occupy a space between light utility aircraft, such as the Cessna C-208, and larger tactical transports such as the C-130. With a stated payload capacity of 3.8 tons and a range of 800 nautical miles, the aircraft is designed for regional cargo distribution rather than long-haul strategic transport.Its short-field capability could let it operate from a wider range of locations, while compatibility with existing cargo infrastructure is intended to simplify integration into logistics networks. These features could be relevant to the US military’s efforts to distribute supplies across dispersed locations without relying entirely on larger transport aircraft.The need is especially pronounced in the Indo-Pacific, where long distances and geographically separated operating sites can complicate fuel supply and resupply. An aircraft that requires less fuel for a given transport task could reduce demand on the logistics network that delivers fuel to forward locations.According to the Air Force’s Associate Deputy Assistant Secretary for Operational Energy, Safety and Occupational Health, Jim Hartle, the funding will help evaluate how a commercially developed aircraft could support distributed logistics while generating data to inform future military requirements.Commercial, defense-readyNatilus is developing KONA for the commercial regional freight market while pursuing potential military applications. The company is advancing the aircraft toward FAA Part 23 certification and full-scale flight testing, with the Air Force funding intended to accelerate its progress toward an operationally relevant demonstration.The project will also let the military assess practical performance, including payload, range, fuel efficiency, reliability, and utilization. These measurements will help establish how the aircraft might perform in real logistics operations, rather than relying solely on design projections.Natilus CEO Aleksey Matyushev said the investment would accelerate the aircraft’s demonstration timeline as the company continues developing it for commercial freight customers.Beyond cargo transport, KONA’s modular architecture and optionally piloted design could eventually support other configurations, including communications relay, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and payload delivery. However, the initial defense focus is regional airlift and contested logistics. The $3.5 million award is a development investment, not confirmation that KONA is ready for military service.

title: US startup to build autonomous nuclear reactor for lunar missions
content: The United States has taken a major step to advance autonomous reactor operation for national security missions. For this, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has awarded Space Nuclear Power Corporation (SpaceNukes) an Other Transaction Agreement (OTA) under the Fast Capacitance (Fat Cat) program. The contract supports development and ground testing of advanced reactor control technologies that extend the demonstrated capability of American nuclear power.Sustained nuclear developmentThe award extends a continuous line of nuclear power development and builds directly on SpaceNukes’ successful nuclear power demonstration heritage. “This award recognizes the maturity and continuity of the team that designed, built, and tested KRUSTY in 2018,” said Patrick McClure, COO of SpaceNukes. In 2018, key members of the SpaceNukes team, while employed by Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA, performed the foundational Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology (KRUSTY) work — conducting the only full-power ground test of a new American space reactor in five decades. “We are proud to work alongside Dr. Dodson and Los Alamos National Laboratory to deliver the next demonstrated step in American nuclear power.”Under the current agreement, SpaceNukes and Los Alamos National Laboratory will design, build, and conduct a follow-on nuclear ground test of a Kilopower reactor incorporating active control rod operation—an advancement beyond the passively controlled architecture demonstrated in the 2018 KRUSTY test. The Fat Cat program seeks to advance autonomous reactor operation for national security missions, according to a press release.Towards autonomous reactor controlThe phased program structure includes design, procurement, and integration gates leading to the ground demonstration, producing both nuclear-tested hardware and the engineering basis for autonomous, actively-controlled reactor operation.Integration work will be conducted at SpaceNukes’ workshop in Medina, Ohio, led by Chief Engineer Marc Gibson. The work positions American industry to provide reliable nuclear power across a broader range of mission profiles, including those requiring dynamic power management and rapid response under varying operational conditions, according to the press statement.“There is no substitute for demonstrated technology when American national security objectives are at stake,” said Andy Phelps, CEO of SpaceNukes. “This award lets us advance the work begun in the KRUSTY program and bring another tested capability forward for the nation.”The technology could have important applications in space exploration, including providing electricity for future Moon bases, scientific instruments and long-duration space missions. Nuclear power can also be useful in locations where sunlight is limited or where solar panels alone may not provide a sufficiently reliable supply of energy. Similar systems could potentially support remote facilities and certain defense applications that require dependable power. However, these are potential applications of the technology rather than confirmation that this specific reactor is ready for operational use.The project is significant because it aims to move beyond demonstrating a small nuclear reactor toward developing a more advanced system capable of actively controlling its own operation. The next steps involve developing the design, integrating the necessary components and conducting ground tests to evaluate the controller’s performance.

title: Diamond quantum sensor could power mind-controlled exoskeletons
content: Scientists in Germany have just presented a new diamond-based quantum sensor that could let people with paralysis control robotic exoskeletons with nothing but the power of their minds.Developed by a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Solid State Physics IAF in Freiburg im Breisgau, the sensor uses a laser system to detect weak magnetic fields with high sensitivity. It achieved 100 percent optical contrast and improved the balance between sensitivity and measurement range by a factor of up to 590 compared with existing technologies.The effort was led by Jan Jeske, PhD, a researcher at Fraunhofer IAF. Jeske, who heads the Quantum Sensing Group at Fraunhofer at the research institute, was the the first to come up with a theoretical model for a magnetic-field-sensitive laser system using diamond with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers a decade ago.“I am very pleased that we have now experimentally demonstrated the magnetic-field-dependent shift in the lasing threshold,” Jeske explained. The sensor could have applications in brain-computer interfaces, medical testing, navigation, and resource exploration.Detecting magnetic fieldsSensors that detect very weak magnetic fields have a limited measurement range. At the same time, those with a wider range are generally less sensitive. This is why the team created a technique called laser threshold magnetometry. It relies on NV centers, which are, in essence, tiny defects in diamond crystals that respond to magnetic fields. An NV center forms when a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom in a diamond, leaving a neighboring spot empty.Conventional diamond quantum sensors measure fluorescent light that is emitted by these defects. The new technology instead places the diamond directly inside a laser cavity. The NV centers interact with the laser’s light field, causing changes in magnetic fields to affect the laser’s output.Under certain conditions, these changes can even turn off the laser and result in 100 percent optical contrast. For comparison, most NV-based magnetic sensors typically achieve just a few percent. The system can produce laser signals with a power of up to 50 milliwatts (mW). These are much stronger than those from conventional sensors.Real-life applicationsCalculations determined that the technology could spot extremely weak magnetic fields, with a sensitivity below 400 femtotesla (fT) per square root of hertz (Hz) for each of the three magnetic-field parts, under ideal photon shot-noise limits.According to the group, apart from improving magnetic-field measurements, the find could also help people living with paralysis. These signals could eventually be transmitted through a brain-computer interface to control robotic exoskeletons.Other possible uses include detecting weak magnetic signals from the heart and muscles, improving navigation, and spotting underground magnetic anomalies. Still, the technology is still under development and has yet to be tested. “Our approach could resolve a trade-off that has long limited the development and application of magnetic-field sensors,” Florian Schall, a PhD researcher at Fraunhofer IAF and the study’s first author, said in a press release. “It could pave the way for a new generation of mobile, highly sensitive magnetic-field sensors.”The study has been published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: US tests SpaceX's rocket capsule to deliver cargo around the world
content: The US Air Force is exploring whether rockets could deliver military cargo anywhere on Earth in a fraction of the time conventional transport takes. On October 20, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) tested cargo-delivery technologies aboard a commercial SpaceX launch, using a Starfall reentry capsule to study how equipment withstands the journey through space and back into the atmosphere.The test is part of AFRL’s Rocket Cargo research program, which aims to determine whether large commercial rockets could rapidly transport tens of tons of supplies to locations around the world, including remote sites and areas where conventional aircraft cannot easily operate.Rather than demonstrating a complete operational delivery system, the latest experiment focused on collecting data about cargo protection during launch and reentry. Researchers loaded the capsule with prototype cargo pods, mission equipment, and sensors to assess the conditions that future payloads would have to survive.Testing whether cargo can survive launch and reentryThe Starfall capsule carried several experimental cargo pods developed by AFRL to accommodate different payloads. Each pod contained representative mission equipment and environmental sensors designed to measure temperature, shock, and vibration during the journey.Researchers paid particular attention to electronics and survival equipment, including batteries, a satellite communications-enabled tracker, a reverse-osmosis water desalination system, emergency medical supplies, and survival gear. Engineers also checked whether a UNI-PAC III life raft would fit inside the capsule, potentially allowing it to be included in future tests.These measurements are important because rocket-based delivery introduces challenges beyond simply reaching a destination quickly. Cargo must withstand the forces of launch, the conditions encountered in space, and the heat and mechanical stresses associated with atmospheric reentry. The equipment must then arrive in a condition suitable for immediate use.AFRL said the experiment would help researchers understand how to protect sensitive equipment during this process. The agency did not announce a timeline for operational deployment or provide a confirmed delivery time for a future end-to-end mission.Why the US military is interested in rocket cargoRocket Cargo is intended to complement conventional military transport rather than simply replace it. AFRL sees a potential advantage in delivering tens of tons of supplies in a single launch, potentially reaching locations without suitable runways or road infrastructure.Such a capability could support military operations in contested environments, where transport aircraft and ground supply routes may face threats or logistical constraints. Potential applications also include expeditionary missions, rescue operations, disaster relief, and responses to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear hazards.The concept remains experimental, however. Launch costs, cargo handling, landing locations, reentry safety, and the ability to deliver supplies reliably at scale are among the practical challenges that any operational system would need to address.AFRL is working with several commercial companies, including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Sierra Space, Anduril, Inversion Space, and Outpost Space, to evaluate launch vehicles and reentry technologies.The latest test is another step toward determining whether commercial space transportation can become a practical tool for military logistics. Right now, the focus remains on gathering data and reducing technical risks before rocket-powered cargo delivery can move from experimental demonstrations toward routine operations.

title: 100-channel single-photon detector opens doors to quantum internet
content: Researchers at the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology (SIMIT) in China have built a 100-channel single-photon detector that opens the door to developing broadband quantum-based networks in China. A prototype network tested with this detector showed communication fidelity of over 90 percent. With advances in quantum computing and sensing technologies, there will soon be a need for a quantum information network. Although different approaches are being tested for such a network, one that closely resembles existing optical fiber networks is likely to be adopted due to its ease of transition. Single-photon detectors or SPDs are critical components of such networks since they facilitate the measurement of photons, or individual light particles, that can be used to store quantum information. SPDs can help in deploying fiber optic or space links for quantum data transfer while also helping facilitate quantum entanglement or teleportation by transferring quantum states to photons. Challenges of using SPDsFor quantum technologies to evolve and scale, we also need to develop SPDs with higher capacities. Currently, there are two types of SPDs that are being used for quantum research. Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), are high-end optoelectronic devices that are extremely precise in their detection but need ultracold temperatures for operation.  Single-Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPADs), on the other hand, can work at room temperature but do not offer high accuracy. This is why SNSPDs are preferred. However, the ultracold temperature requirements of SNSPDs present other challenges. For readouts, the SNSPDs are connected to instruments that are maintained at room temperature. This is achieved with coaxial cables that are relatively thick and built with thermally conductive metals. These cables allow room-temperature heat to travel into the cryogenic chamber where the SNSPD operates; this is known as thermal load. As the number of detection channels inside a SNSPD increases, the number of cables needed to read out the signals also increases, which then increases the thermal load. The workaround for this has been to limit the number of detectors to 32, which is the standard when it comes to SPDs. A 100-channel SPD To overcome this, researchers at SIMIT performed a comprehensive redesign of the SNSPD and replaced the coaxial cables with special flexible materials called high-density multi-core microstrip lines. These lines are not just ultrathin but also thermally insulating, so the heat they send back to the cryogenic chamber is minimal. According to the SIMIT team, the heat that entered the system was one twenty-first that of the traditional cables. This allowed them to add more independent channels to the SPD while also maintaining long-term stability and not significantly increasing the size of the SPD. To test their design, the researchers ran the SPD round the clock for seven days and yet the temperature of the cryogenic chamber stayed below 2.1K, very close to the absolute zero temperature of 0K (-273.15 degrees Celsius). During the test, the channels demonstrated detection efficiency of 80 percent while also reporting extremely low false positives, the researchers noted in a paper. For a more real-world scenario comparison, the team built a five-user quantum entanglement distribution network with 10 two-way quantum links. Each user received photons using the newly developed channels of the SPD, and communication fidelity, or the preservation of quantum information, was found to be more than 90 percent, the paper added. The research findings were published in the journal Laser & Photonics Reviews.

title: US: 2.5 GW hybrid nuclear plant using 1,500-ton blocks slated for Texas
content: Stepping up the country’s nuclear energy goals, the American government has greenlit another clean energy project.A hybrid nuclear power plant with 2.5 gigawatt (GW) energy capacity will be up and running in Victoria, Texas, in less than five years. The project would break free from historic nuclear construction timelines, which typically take more than 10 years to complete.To reduce those delays, the government has backed clean-tech startup Blue Energy, which expects to shorten construction time to about 36 months.Blocks at shipyardsTo minimize the cost and construction period, the company will manufacture prefabricated reactor sections, called “Blue Blocks,” at shipyards. Built using conventional reactor designs, each block will weigh around 1,500 tons, the company claimed, and can be transported directly from the shipyard and assembled at the nuclear plant site within a year.“The 1,500-ton Blue Block prefabricated modules are fully functional mechanically and electrically, they have plumbing — everything is delivered ready to run directly to the site,” said Blue Energy founder and CEO Jake Jurewicz.Recognizing that the “nuclear problem is a construction problem,” Jurewicz said the company plans to leverage the existing manufacturing supply base used by offshore oil, gas, and wind industries that operate from shipyards.The company said building at shipyards offers several advantages, including access to a large skilled workforce, specialized infrastructure, and greater opportunities for automation because manufacturing takes place under controlled conditions.The Blue Blocks will house small modular light-water reactors supplied by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy.Switch from gas to nuclearBeyond shipyard construction and prefabricated modules, the company also plans to operate its plants on natural gas initially before transitioning to nuclear reactors, a strategy aimed at reducing costs and avoiding project delays.“We have this gas-to-nuclear technology that allows us to get things going earlier with gas by building the whole nuclear steam turbine system right away,” said Jurewicz.Using this approach, the company expects not only to bring the plant online sooner but also to begin generating revenue within three years of the start of construction.“By energizing it with steam from gas combustion turbines, which means we can finance it as a gas plant, so the cost of capital goes down,” he added.According to Jurewicz, the approach dramatically lowers project costs while reducing financial risk. The company has already received approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for its gas-to-nuclear strategy.Under the plan, Blue Energy’s first Texas power plant will begin operating in 2030 with two gas turbines producing 1 GW of electricity. Two years later, the facility will reach its full 2.5 GW capacity by adding up to five small modular reactors, generating an additional 1.5 GW of power.For future projects, the company expects to reduce construction costs to as low as $5,000 per kilowatt, delivering electricity at less than half the cost of existing nuclear plants.The modular design will also make it easier to add more reactors at the Texas site in the future while supporting community needs such as desalination.“This power infrastructure is clean, reliable, and resilient through hurricanes or any other weather scenario that can happen in that community,” Jurewicz added.

title: 95% of fine air pollution removed by new car technology while driving
content: Cars could help clean the air along the roads they travel, with researchers in South Korea developing a vehicle system that captures airborne particles and collects brake dust before it escapes into the surroundings.A team led by Dr. Bangwoo Han at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM) tested the technology on vehicles including a Kia Carnival and Hyundai Sonata. The approach integrates pollution control into existing vehicle components, addressing both roadside particulate matter and particles generated during braking.Turning grille into air filterThe grille-mounted system uses electrostatic precipitation to collect particles from incoming air. It electrically charges the particles, then attracts them to collection plates.Carbon fibers much thinner than a human hair enable collection using low electrical current while minimizing ozone generation. During driving, airflow from the vehicle’s movement carries air through the system, eliminating the need for a separate high-power blower.Tests showed that the grille system removed at least 95 percent of PM2.5 and at least 99 percent of particles in the PM2.5–10 range at 18.64 miles per hour (mph). It maintained those removal levels at 31 mph and purified about 1,000 cubic feet of air per vehicle per minute.Fuel efficiency changes after installation and remained within 1 percent for both vehicle models.Capturing brake particles at sourceA second collection device sits behind the brake caliper, capturing particles produced by friction between the brake pads and discs.These particles naturally acquire an electric charge during braking. The system uses that charge to collect them without a separate particle charger or suction fan.Under the Worldwide harmonized Light vehicles Test Cycle (WLTC), the collector captured over 35 milligrams of brake wear particles per mile per vehicle. That corresponds to approximately 0.35 ounces over nearly 280 miles.“A key feature of this technology is that vehicles can remove fine particulate matter from roadside air while also reducing brake wear particles directly at the source,” Han said.“By linking this technology with AirFive, one of KIMM’s Five Flagship Brands, we plan to expand its application to help improve urban air quality,” he added. Cleaning air while parkedThe technology also includes wireless power transfer for air purification while parked. In a parking space equipped with wireless power, the vehicle’s existing radiator fan can draw surrounding air through the purification system.The research addresses non-exhaust pollution, which remains relevant to electric and hydrogen-powered vehicles because they also generate particles from brakes and tires. KIMM’s approach targets roadside airborne particles and brake wear, with the institute highlighting its relevance to Euro 7 brake particle regulations.“By utilizing the vehicle’s existing structure and airflow generated during driving, we minimized the need for additional power,” said Dr. Gun Hee Lee, a senior researcher at KIMM.“Having verified the technology through vehicle testing, we plan to further validate its performance and long-term durability under real-world driving conditions,” he added.The research received support through the Automotive Industry Core Technology Development Program. Related findings have appeared in journals including Tribology International and Atmosphere, and multiple patent applications have been filed in South Korea, the United States, and Germany.

title: 2,000 MW underground nuclear reactors eyed for former US munitions site
content: A former munitions depot in Kansas is set to host an unusual nuclear energy project. Energy startup Deep Fission has signed a major supply deal with the Great Plains Development Authority. The firm plans to provide up to 2,000 megawatts of electricity to the Great Plains Industrial Park in Parsons.The project eliminates traditional above-ground reactor domes. Instead, engineers plan to install reactors in boreholes about one mile beneath the surface.The agreement turns an earlier letter of intent into a binding commercial contract. Local officials hope guaranteed, low-carbon power will attract heavy industry to the 14,000-acre site.“Dependable, affordable power is what draws employers to Southeast Kansas, and it’s what the companies we’re talking to are asking for,” said Brad Reams, director of the park. “Deep Fission’s Gravity reactor is designed to provide firm, carbon-free electricity right here at the park, and this agreement gives us a long-term energy plan to offer.”Using a proprietary designThe project uses Deep Fission’s proprietary design, named the Gravity reactor. In basic terms, it is a pressurized water reactor. It runs on standard low-enriched uranium fuel, just like commercial plants operating worldwide.The critical difference is its working environment. Traditional reactors use massive concrete containment domes and pressurizer vessels that keep the cooling water under intense pressure.Deep Fission replaces those mechanical systems with natural geology. The reactor sits inside a narrow, water-filled shaft deep underground. At a depth of one mile, the weight of the water column creates intense pressure. This natural hydrostatic pressure keeps the coolant water liquid at high temperatures.At the same time, the surrounding bedrock acts as an immense radiation shield. The surrounding rock and water also absorb heat and provide passive emergency cooling.The company says this layout removes the need for large surface structures. By using standard commercial drilling rigs, Deep Fission aims to lower building costs and speed up deployment.Testing for commercial rolloutField trials have already started. In September, crews lowered a full-scale 20-foot canister 100 feet down a test borehole. The team aligned the unit at depth and hauled it back up to test the deployment equipment before attempting deeper drilling.Parsons began work under a Department of Energy pilot initiative. With the supply contract signed, the project now moves toward commercial delivery.Phase one targets 150 megawatts. Once licensed and operational, Deep Fission plans to start commercial operations by September 30, 2028. After that, capacity will scale up in steps to match local demand, eventually reaching 2,000 megawatts.The local authority will purchase power to meet the energy needs of its commercial tenants. It also has the right to enter into purchase agreements directly with individual businesses. The contract carries no minimum purchase quota for the park authority.“This agreement turns a shared vision into a binding commitment,” concluded Liz Muller, chief executive of Deep Fission. “Our approach is to bring firm power directly to where it’s needed.”

title: 725 MW US nuclear plant recovers tilted fuel with custom-build device
content: A shuttered nuclear power plant in the US has overcome a major challenge ahead of its planned restart after engineers successfully recovered a tilted fuel assembly from its reactor.The demanding operation was carried out at the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant in Michigan. Florida-based energy technology firm, Holtec International announced its successful completion Wednesday, October 21.For the procedure, the company used a specially designed Fuel Movement Device (FMD), which it developed, manufactured, and delivered in just two weeks. According to Holtec, the feat brings the nuclear plant closer to restarting operations.The facility could become the first permanently shut-down US commercial nuclear plant to return to power generation. The fuel recovery was reportedly carried out safely and without errors. “When we encounter a challenge, what matters is how we respond,” Fadi Diya, Holtec International chief nuclear officer, said. Rapid device developmentThe facility’s restart preparations were temporarily disrupted on August 30, 2026, after a fuel bundle unexpectedly tilted at a 30-degree angle inside the reactor. Its bottom remained in position H-1, and its top leaned against the core shroud. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), confirmed that the incident caused no radiation release or worker injuries.However, recovering the tilted fuel assembly required a specialized engineering solution. To address the challenge, Holtec developed a custom Fuel Movement Device and a specially engineered fuel transfer canister to safely lift, secure, and relocate the assembly.Fuel assembly is moved through the equipment hatch using Holtec’s Fuel Transfer Canister for storage in the spent fuel pool.Credit: Holtec InternationalThe equipment was developed in Camden, New Jersey, while the specialized parts were produced in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. At the same time, Palisades personnel handled the regulatory preparations, equipment testing, training, as well as the recovery operation.Once the equipment was ready technical crews lifted the tilted fuel assembly from the reactor and placed it in a specially designed container. The team then secured the lid and moved the container to the plant’s spent fuel pool. Holtec stated that the recovered assembly is now safely stored in the pool.Restart efforts continueThe NRC approved the recovery procedure through a license amendment. “Our team approached this recovery with the same commitment to safety, technical rigor, and teamwork that has guided our work throughout the restart,” Diya said.The Michigan plant previously ceased operations in 2022 and is now undergoing preparations to return to commercial electricity generation. Its restart would be the first of its kind in US nuclear history.Holtec’s specially-designed Fuel Movement Device staged above the reactor to undertake fuel recovery.Credit: Holtec InternationalHowever, the reactor is not ready yet. Workers still need to complete fuel loading, inspections, and safety tests. Holtec must also meet federal regulations. The firm said its experience with nuclear fuel supported the recovery.“We developed a solution, executed it safely and error-free, and demonstrated the depth of expertise across our organization,” Diya shared in a press release. “I’m proud of this team and grateful for the dedication they bring to Palisades every day.”
