title: US firm taps NVIDIA stacks for 50% gain in quantum error decoding
content: Quantum computers need to correct errors without slowing their calculations to a crawl. Now, quantum computing company SEEQC says it has demonstrated an architecture that improved two key quantum error-correction decoding metrics by approximately 50% by combining specialized chip-based processing with NVIDIA’s quantum computing software and GPU infrastructure.The results combine SEEQC’s chip-based pre-decoder technology with NVIDIA Ising, an open family of AI models that includes tools for quantum error correction, and NVIDIA NVQLink, an interface designed to connect quantum processors with GPU-accelerated computing systems.The demonstration used a simulated quantum processor and system architecture incorporating realistic decoder latency at scale. It compared the combined architecture with NVIDIA Ising operating as a standalone pre-decoder. SEEQC reported an approximately 50% reduction in decoding latency and improved logical error-rate performance.The results could point toward a way to reduce one of the major bottlenecks in building fault-tolerant quantum computers: processing error-correction information quickly enough to keep increasingly complex quantum systems operating reliably.Why quantum computers need faster error correctionQuantum computers use qubits, which can represent quantum information in ways that differ from conventional binary bits. However, qubits are highly susceptible to disturbances from their environment and imperfections in control operations. These errors can accumulate and undermine a computation.Quantum error correction addresses this problem by encoding information across multiple physical qubits and using measurements to detect errors without directly measuring and destroying the encoded quantum information. Classical computing systems then process those measurements to determine which corrections are needed.That classical processing stage is known as decoding. As quantum processors grow, the volume of information to be processed can increase substantially, putting pressure on the time and computing resources available for error correction.Two important measures are decoding latency, the time required to process error information, and logical error rate, which describes how often an encoded logical qubit experiences an error. Reducing both could help make fault-tolerant quantum computing more practical.Bringing specialized processing closer to the qubitsSEEQC’s approach uses a chip-based pre-decoder to handle part of the decoding workload closer to the quantum processing unit (QPU). The system then uses NVIDIA Ising’s decoding capabilities, leveraging SEEQC’s Digital Link and NVIDIA NVQLink to provide a low-latency communication framework between quantum and GPU-accelerated computing environments.The idea is to process some information locally before sending it to higher-level classical computing resources. This could reduce the amount of data that needs to move between components while accelerating time-sensitive operations.The distinction matters because quantum computers cannot scale simply by adding more qubits. Their supporting electronics, communication links, and classical processing systems must also keep pace. Moving selected processing tasks closer to the QPU could help reduce the time and infrastructure overhead required to correct errors as systems grow.SEEQC CEO John Levy said the results demonstrate how digital chip technology could improve the interface between quantum processors and high-performance computing infrastructure. NVIDIA’s quantum product director, Sam Stanwyck, said the work shows how open models and interfaces can help quantum hardware developers combine specialized processing with AI and GPU computing.What the results mean for fault-tolerant quantum computingThe reported 50% improvement is promising, but it needs to be understood in context. The experiment used a simulated quantum processor and architecture stack, rather than demonstrating the same performance gains on a fully operational physical quantum computer. The announcement also does not establish that the improvement will translate directly into a 50% reduction in the total resources required to build a fault-tolerant system.Instead, the results provide evidence that distributing decoding tasks between specialized chip-based processing and GPU-accelerated computing may improve key parts of the error-correction pipeline.SEEQC says its next step is to integrate the system-level components demonstrated so far and work toward chip-to-chip integration of a quantum processor with advanced high-performance computing infrastructure. The company also plans to investigate further opportunities to improve quantum error correction and other hybrid quantum-classical workloads.Ultimately, practical fault-tolerant quantum computing will require advances across the entire system, from qubits and control electronics to communication and decoding. The SEEQC-NVIDIA demonstration addresses one part of that challenge, showing how tighter hardware and software integration could help quantum systems scale more efficiently.

title: 50 AI agents built a working society on four gaming GPUs, reproducing an MIT study
content: Give 50 AI agents a shared world, no roles and no instructions, and they will start building technology together. That was the central finding of SwarmWorld, a study published in August by MIT’s Laboratory for Atomistic and Molecular Mechanics. The original work ran on a hosted frontier model.Now a team working with Apex Fusion Foundation, a Swiss foundation building infrastructure for AI agents, has reproduced that experiment on four Nvidia RTX 3090 cards, the kind found in high-end gaming PCs. Using MIT’s code and commands unchanged, the run took about 26 hours and 12,800 model calls.How the MIT experiment worksIn SwarmWorld, researchers Pal, Wang and Buehler placed 50 or more language-model agents in a shared simulated world. None had an assigned job or a recipe to follow. The agents explored, gathered materials, ran tests and built persistent technologies. Some wrote programs that kept running after the agents themselves were removed.The agents rarely needed to talk to each other. They coordinated by leaving changes in the world for others to find and build on, a process biologists call stigmergy, the same mechanism ants use when they lay pheromone trails.The societies built broader and more resilient portfolios of technology than the best of an equal number of agents working alone. They also split into specialist roles, such as builders and explorers, without being told to. MIT released its code, prompts and complete traces, which made an outside check possible.Swapping the frontier model for a 27B oneThe replication, led by Časlav Nedeljković of HAL8, asked whether a small lab could get the same result with open weights on hardware it owns. The team used Qwen3.8-27B, an open-weight model compressed to 4-bit precision so it would fit across four 24 GB consumer cards.Nine of MIT’s 12 paired effects matched in direction, including every gain in portfolio resilience. Two of those three gains came out larger than in the original. The remaining three fell within noise. The agents also self-organized as before, with societies that shared culture clustering around their technologies. MIT’s own analysis tools, run on the new traces, drew the same picture.The smaller model was a weaker individual and a stronger teammate.ModelSolo agent (research milestones)Society (research milestones)MIT’s hosted frontier model7 to 10 of 1614 of 16Qwen3.8-27B, 4-bit6 of 1616 of 16“MIT released everything a second lab needs to check its work, and that made this possible,” Nedeljković said. “We changed the model, the precision and the hardware, and the central result still held. “The society gap widened with a weaker model, which suggests the collective effect is robust.”That conclusion rests on a single run at one population size. The larger populations in MIT’s study haven’t been rerun yet.A hidden setting that mattered more than model sizeThe replication also surfaced two findings for engineers building agent systems.The first concerns the KV cache, the memory a language model uses to hold the context of a conversation while it generates text. Serving software often stores this cache at reduced numerical precision to save GPU memory. In the replication, changing that precision moved results more than the gap between a 27B and a 235B model. Agent benchmarks run on self-hosted hardware may therefore reflect serving configuration as much as model choice.The second is an audit of MIT’s own data. The released traces reproduce every observable event and metric in the original study, with the exception of one internal check. The team sent both findings to the MIT authors with supporting evidence, as a GitHub issue and a pull request.Keeping a ledger of agent workApex Fusion’s interest in the study goes beyond reproducibility. Once agents from different organizations work together, tracking which agent did the work, what it was worth and whether the record can be checked later becomes an engineering problem in its own right.Its answer is Vector, which it describes as a settlement layer for AI agents, where each agent carries an identity and every job ends with a signed receipt recorded on a blockchain.The replication itself ran directly on the team’s own GPUs. The team also registered its model server as a supplier on the Vector marketplace, an OpenAI-compatible gateway that meters each request and settles usage on-chain in AP3X, the network’s utility token. A 32-call pilot through Vector behaved the same as the direct run.“As AI agents from different organizations start working together, the most valuable thing in the system is a trustworthy record of who did what,” said Christopher Greenwood, CEO of Apex Fusion Foundation.Whether multi-organization agent networks need a blockchain for that record, rather than conventional logging and billing, is still an open question, and the replication itself doesn’t settle it.What’s nextThe team is now running a full side-by-side comparison of the direct and Vector runs, along with the next population size from MIT’s study. Activity on the Vector network can be followed on a live dashboard. The replication paper and every trace from the experiment are published on Hugging Face for anyone to check.The broader point may be the one MIT’s Markus Buehler raised in August: when agents coordinate through changes to a shared environment, watching their messages to each other isn’t enough. If societies like these can run on four gaming GPUs, that is no longer a concern only for frontier labs.

title: Video: Tiny robots steal the show at NVIDIA event with funny stumbles
content: Four robots, roughly 10 inches tall, walked onto Nvidia’s GTC Berlin stage on Wednesday evening, then sat, tumbled, and attempted somersaults. The demonstration introduced Microduck, a small biped developed by Pollen Robotics.Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang guided the robots through several commands, showing how machines weighing less than two pounds each could move and respond during a live presentation. Their performance included successful rolls, missed instructions, and recoveries after falling.The demonstration also highlighted the computing behind those movements. According to Huang, the robots were trained in the cloud using large Nvidia systems, with their movements refined inside an Omniverse digital twin running on an RTX Spark machine.Walking, tumbling, and getting back upThe four Microducks initially walked out on their own. Huang greeted them, asked them to sit, and then instructed them to stand again.A request to take a nap produced a less orderly response. Three robots promptly tipped onto the floor, while the fourth continued walking for a few more steps before falling onto its side.Huang laughed and encouraged the machines to get back up before asking them to somersault. A couple completed the movement, while others remained in place or needed further encouragement.One robot wandered farther away, tripped, and righted itself. Huang then called it back: “Pay attention. Stay focused. Come here.”The Microduck eventually approached and sat down, drawing more laughter from the audience. The sequence showed both the movements the robots could perform and the uneven responses that accompanied their live appearance.Fifteen motors and an articulated beakEach Microduck contains 15 motors distributed across its legs, neck, and head. Its onboard equipment also includes a front camera, a depth sensor, and two small inertial measurement units.An articulated beak gives the robot another function beyond walking and posing: it can pick up relatively light objects from the ground.The robot can walk, sit, and crouch, and it can recover after falls. Attaching wheels also allows it to roller-skate.The stage demonstration focused on several of these physical abilities, particularly walking, sitting, rolling, and returning upright. Although some commands produced immediate responses, others required repeated encouragement. Huang also used the appearance to discuss Europe’s history of producing precision-engineered products, pointing to the Microducks as an example.Initial batch sells out before deliveriesMicroduck was initially offered at $399 before taxes and shipping, but that purchasing window has already closed, with the robots sold out. First shipments are expected to arrive by Christmas in North America and Europe. The available colors are Cream, Graphite, Lavender, and Sky.The four robots appeared together during the presentation, giving the audience a look at multiple units responding to the same instructions. Their differing reactions became a recurring feature of the demonstration. Some sat or rolled when asked, while others paused, wandered, or fell. Together, those moments put the small robots’ movement capabilities on display, alongside the occasional stumble that came with performing them live onstage.

title: 6.6 GW nuclear power campus proposed in US state with six reactors
content: Eastern Kentucky could host the largest nuclear power campus in the United States under a proposal to expand American electricity production and rebuild the country’s capacity to build nuclear plants at scale.The Nuclear Company has announced Prosperity One, a proposed development along the Ohio River in Lewis County that could accommodate up to six Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. Together, the reactors would generate approximately 6.6 gigawatts of electricity if fully constructed. The company, which has site control in the area, plans to pursue federal approvals to begin construction in 2028. It is working with local landowners and community leaders to advance a project intended to bring industrial investment, skilled jobs, and long-term economic opportunities to the region.A push to build nuclear at scaleThe company frames Prosperity One as a response to President Donald Trump’s call to accelerate American energy production. If fully completed, the proposed campus would also rank among the largest nuclear power campuses worldwide, according to the announcement.“For generations, communities along the Ohio River have formed America’s industrial backbone,” said Joe Klecha, chief nuclear officer for The Nuclear Company.“We are proud to partner with the community to apply our team’s collective experience to deliver lasting jobs, a stronger tax base, and reliable power for Kentucky,” he added. Klecha brings 33 years of nuclear experience, including service aboard US Navy nuclear submarines and leadership positions in nuclear fleet operations. He also led construction and operational readiness at Vogtle Units 3 and 4.The company said its Services division has performed maintenance at more than 40 percent of America’s currently operating nuclear power facilities.Local jobs drive community interestSite owner and lifelong Lewis County resident Sam Howard has partnered with the company to advance the development, citing opportunities for future generations.“I have nine grandchildren, and all of them live in Lewis County. I want them to have the opportunity to stay,” said Howard.“For years, our county’s unemployment rate has been among the highest in the state. An infrastructure project like this could provide jobs and economic opportunities for generations of Eastern Kentucky residents. I am proud to help advance this development,” he added. Lewis County is also seeking designation as a nuclear-ready community under the Kentucky Nuclear Energy Development Authority.County leaders unanimously launched that effort in July 2026. Following public input meetings, they voted overwhelmingly earlier this month to submit the county’s filing to the authority.Studies and licensing come nextThe Nuclear Company is preparing the engineering, environmental, regulatory, and commercial work needed to move Prosperity One toward construction. Initial activities include detailed site characterization, geotechnical investigations, environmental assessments, transmission interconnection planning, and preparation for federal nuclear licensing.Planning will also address transportation, housing, environmental stewardship, emergency preparedness, and water use, along with other considerations for a development of this scale. The company plans to engage the Nuclear Regulatory Commission through its established licensing processes. Its targeted 2028 construction start remains dependent on obtaining the necessary federal approvals.

title: Unitree unveils humanoid robot designed to act as real-life guardian
content: China’s Unitree Robotics has unveiled the H2-X, a humanoid robot designed to help in emergencies, including confronting attackers and rescuing people from danger. A promotional video released on Wednesday shows the robot disarming a knife-wielding intruder, smashing a car door, lifting a vehicle to free a trapped victim, and pulling a pedestrian away from an oncoming car. The demonstration highlighted the company’s efforts to explore practical applications for its robots beyond entertainment and viral stunts. However, Unitree has provided limited details about the H2-X’s technical specifications, availability, and potential commercial deployment.Robot tackles emergenciesUnitree has unveiled the H2-X humanoid robot in a demonstration showing it disarming a knife-wielding attacker, lifting a car, and pulling a pedestrian away from an oncoming vehicle.The Hangzhou-based company released the promotional video on October 21, presenting the machine as a “guardian” robot capable of intervening in dangerous situations. The demonstration shows the H2-X confronting an intruder threatening a woman, smashing through a car door, and moving a person away from the path of an approaching vehicle.However, Unitree has not disclosed detailed technical specifications for the new model or clarified whether the actions demonstrated were performed autonomously or choreographed in advance.The H2-X, presented as “Kung Fu Legend: Guardian,” builds on the company’s existing H2 humanoid platform. Unitree has increasingly used demonstrations of physical capabilities to showcase its robots, including martial arts movements, dancing, acrobatics, and combat-style maneuvers.Unitree’s existing H2 humanoid stands approximately 1.8 meters tall and weighs around 154 pounds (70 kilograms). According to the company’s product description, the earlier model has 31 degrees of freedom and a maximum leg-joint torque of 360 newton-meters.Degrees of freedom indicate the number of independent movements a robotic system can perform. In a humanoid robot, these movements allow different joints to coordinate actions such as walking, turning, balancing, and manipulating objects.Joint torque is also important for physical tasks, as it determines the rotational force a motor can apply. However, maximum joint torque alone does not establish how much weight a robot can lift, carry, or move under different operating conditions.Unitree has not confirmed whether the H2-X retains the H2’s specifications or uses modified actuators, joints, sensors, or control systems. The company said the newer model could stand for about eight hours, but it did not provide further details on battery capacity, power consumption, or endurance during physically demanding tasks.The company also did not announce a release date or price, leaving questions unanswered about the robot’s availability and intended customers.Robot threat detectionA central technical question is whether the H2-X can recognize threats and respond independently. Although the promotional video depicts the robot intervening in several dangerous situations, Unitree has not explained how it detects people, identifies potential threats, plans movements, or determines when to act.The company has also not clarified whether the robot relies on remote control, pre-programmed sequences, autonomous decision-making, or a combination of these approaches.These distinctions are important for a machine intended to operate around people. Responding to an unexpected attack or moving a person away from a vehicle requires more than physical strength. A robot would need to interpret changing surroundings, coordinate its movements, and avoid causing additional harm.Last month, Unitree announced its UnifoLM-X2-1.0 artificial intelligence model, which it said enabled humanoid robots to spar autonomously by punching, blocking, and dodging. The H2-X demonstration follows this push to combine physical robotics with AI-driven movement and control.Unitree ended the promotional video with a warning against dangerous modifications and unauthorized uses. It advised maintaining a safety distance of at least two to three meters from the robot.The company has not provided evidence establishing the H2-X’s performance in unscripted emergencies. Its practical capabilities, safety safeguards, and readiness for real-world deployment therefore remain unclear.

title: NASA's four-drone Moon mission clears key spacecraft design milestone
content: Firefly Aerospace has completed a key spacecraft design review for a NASA mission that aims to deploy four robotic drones above the Moon’s south pole by late 2028.The Texas-based space company announced on October 21 that its Elytra spacecraft had passed a preliminary design review (PDR) for NASA’s MoonFall mission. The milestone clears the way for the next design phase before hardware production and assembly.The spacecraft will transport drones developed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) from Earth orbit to lunar orbit before releasing them above the Moon’s south pole. The drones are intended to survey terrain, identify potential landing sites, and locate resources for future human missions.The review involved engineers from Firefly, NASA and JPL, who assessed whether the spacecraft’s proposed systems could meet mission requirements. Firefly said it completed the review less than four months after receiving its contract.Spacecraft systems pass scrutinyThe review examined Elytra’s structural design, thermal management, propulsion, avionics, navigation, communications and control systems. Engineers also evaluated plans for qualification and environmental testing.These systems will play different roles during the mission. Propulsion will move the spacecraft toward the Moon, while guidance and navigation systems will help control its trajectory and position. Thermal systems will protect equipment against temperature extremes in space.Communications systems will support contact with mission controllers, while the spacecraft’s control systems will coordinate operations during the journey and deployment.Firefly said the review confirmed that Elytra’s design meets mission requirements. However, this was a design assessment rather than a demonstration of flight-ready hardware.The company will now prepare for its critical design review (CDR), a more detailed evaluation intended to establish whether the spacecraft is ready to move toward manufacturing.“Completing PDR less than four months after contract award is a testament to the speed and rigor Firefly brings to every mission,” said Ray Allensworth, vice president of spacecraft at Firefly Aerospace.Four drones target southNASA’s MoonFall mission is intended to gather information about the lunar south pole, a region being considered for future human exploration and infrastructure development.JPL is responsible for building the four drones and managing the mission, while NASA will arrange the launch vehicle. Firefly will provide the spacecraft needed to transport and deploy the drones.After launch, Elytra is expected to travel from Earth orbit to lunar orbit. It will then release the drones above the lunar south pole, where they are planned to conduct surveys using high-definition optical cameras and other instruments.The observations could help mission planners identify safer landing locations and map resources needed for future lunar operations. Such information would be useful for selecting sites where spacecraft, equipment, and eventually astronauts could operate.MoonFall is part of the initial phase of NASA’s broader Moon Base initiative, which aims to support a sustained human presence and expand scientific and commercial activity near the lunar south pole.Firefly is targeting launch readiness by late 2028. The company has not yet demonstrated the MoonFall drone deployment, and the spacecraft must still complete its final design review, manufacturing, assembly, and testing before launch.

title: Claude Duet taps 6,000-plus integrations to automate business tasks
content: Anthropic wants Claude to do more than answer questions. Its new app, Claude Duet, can work through a user’s backlog, monitor connected accounts, and prepare deliverables without waiting for constant instructions. The research preview targets professionals and small business owners who spend much of their day managing competing priorities.The idea is to give users an assistant that knows when to surface a problem and when to handle routine work independently. Anthropic describes the approach as a matter of judgment, not simply executing commands. The app runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and is available through iOS, Android, and claude.ai.Anthropic says Claude Duet is designed to help people reclaim time for work that demands their attention. Access currently requires joining a waitlist. The preview is included with Pro and Max subscriptions, sharing their existing usage limits.Work that runs unattendedClaude Duet gets its own virtual machine and browser, allowing it to continue working after users leave their devices. Someone could assign a project before stepping away and return to a completed result or a request for approval.Its assignments extend well beyond sorting an inbox. Claude Duet can schedule meetings, prepare financial forecasts, build dashboards, prototype products, and develop web applications. It can also check connected accounts every few hours and send notifications when something needs attention.That monitoring schedule matters because constant checks would consume subscription limits more quickly. Users can also specify which developments deserve a notification and how often the assistant should contact them.Anthropic’s Boris Cherny, who leads the Claude Code team, uses the app to talk through his mental to-do list during walks. Chelsea Larsson, who leads model and product behavior design, hands it her tasks before spending time with her children. Claude Duet then prepares results for an evening report.Connected to business toolsThe app can access more than 6,000 connectors and plugins through the Claude Marketplace. That opens up workflows across communication, finance, recruitment, marketing, and online retail.Claude Duet can find unanswered Gmail messages, draft replies, and identify unpaid invoices in QuickBooks or Stripe. It can prepare payroll details in Gusto and draft job listings for LinkedIn. Teams can also use it to prepare agreements through DocuSign or develop campaigns in Canva.Retailers get Shopify management tools, with a richer storefront editor planned for a future release. Anthropic also supports purchases through Stripe’s Link wallet and Shopify’s Shop Pay. Integration with saved 1Password logins is planned.Users retain final approvalGiving software access to business accounts raises an obvious question about control. Anthropic says Claude Duet must show users its proposed action before sending messages, making payments, signing documents, or deleting data.Some actions remain prohibited even when a user approves them, including securities trading and transfers between accounts. Users can also disconnect applications whenever they choose.Anthropic has added safeguards against malicious instructions hidden in online content. A dedicated classifier and system prompt also restrict the disclosure of sensitive information. The system blocks requests to share highly confidential details, such as credit card numbers and government identification. It allows disclosures involving health or personal finances only when users explicitly authorize them.The company says external penetration testing and adversarial exercises have tested its security infrastructure. Claude Duet also falls under Anthropic’s public bug bounty program.For now, the research preview will test whether an assistant can reliably distinguish between work it should handle and decisions that still need a human.

title: New modular turboprop engine delivers 33% more power, 20% less fuel
content: Pratt & Whitney Canada has introduced a new turboprop engine that promises substantially more power at high altitudes while using less fuel. Called the PT9, the engine delivers 33 percent more power at altitude and cuts fuel consumption by 20 percent compared with previous-generation engines. Transport Canada recently certified the design, marking a key step toward production.The PT9 could interest aircraft operators who need stronger high-altitude performance without accepting a corresponding increase in fuel consumption. Pratt & Whitney Canada also designed the engine to support future propulsion technologies, including hybrid-electric aircraft. The manufacturer is part of RTX, the US-based aerospace and defense group.More power, less fuelThe PT9’s performance gains center on its ability to deliver more power at altitude. Aircraft engines can face demanding operating conditions as air density decreases with increasing elevation. Additional available power can help aircraft maintain performance in those environments.Pratt & Whitney Canada says the PT9 reduces fuel consumption by 20 percent against engines from the previous generation. That improvement could help operators manage fuel costs, particularly on missions that demand sustained power. However, the manufacturer has not disclosed the specific aircraft or operating conditions behind its comparative figures.The engine has accumulated more than 14,000 hours of development work. That effort preceded its recent certification by Transport Canada, Canada’s national civil aviation regulator. Certification clears an important regulatory hurdle, although the announcement does not specify a production delivery schedule or a launch customer.Designed for future aircraftThe PT9 uses a new architectural approach that combines turboprop efficiency with performance characteristics associated with jet propulsion. Pratt & Whitney Canada has also incorporated advanced digital capabilities into the design. Its modular construction allows engineers to adapt the platform and integrate additional technologies over time.That flexibility could prove important as aircraft manufacturers explore hybrid-electric propulsion. Such systems combine conventional thermal engines with electric power components to improve how aircraft generate and use energy. Pratt & Whitney Canada says the PT9’s architecture can accommodate future hybrid thermal-electric configurations.The manufacturer also intends the engine to serve different airframe designs. That adaptability could broaden its potential applications, although Pratt & Whitney Canada has not announced specific aircraft programs for the PT9.Satheeshkumar Kumarasingam, president of Pratt & Whitney Canada, described the engine as the next stage in turboprop propulsion. He said its design reflects changing customer requirements and supports continued technology integration.Production planned in AlbertaPratt & Whitney Canada plans to manufacture the PT9 in Lethbridge, Alberta. The facility also serves as the company’s global center of excellence for the PT6 family of turboprop engines.The PT6 is an established engine family, giving the Lethbridge site an existing connection to turboprop manufacturing. The PT9 will add a new platform to that production base, with an architecture intended to accommodate future developments.The engine’s certification establishes a foundation for its next steps, but several details remain undisclosed. Pratt & Whitney Canada has yet to identify the PT9’s first aircraft application or provide a timeline for deliveries. Those details will help clarify how quickly the new engine can move from development into operational service.

title: NVIDIA tech cuts humanoid robot processing delay by 8x in tests
content: Bear Robotics says it has reduced the time needed to run a robotics foundation model by roughly eight times, from 500 milliseconds to 60 milliseconds, using NVIDIA software on its KR1 humanoid robot.The improvement comes through KINO-2, a new robot-learning platform designed to turn human demonstrations into tasks that KR1 can perform. The company reported a separate 4.2-fold improvement for its own model, reducing processing time from 72.3 milliseconds to 17.2 milliseconds.The figures come from Bear’s internal measurements and refer to model inference, the process of generating an output from a trained model. They do not mean the robot moves eight times faster or completes physical tasks eight times sooner.Bear Robotics, which develops robots for commercial operations, announced KINO-2 at NVIDIA GTC Berlin. The company says it has deployed more than 16,000 robots across over 5,000 customer locations, although most of those machines are service robots rather than humanoids.Cutting robot response delaysKINO-2 is designed to help KR1 learn object-handling tasks from demonstrations instead of requiring engineers to program every movement separately.Bear collects demonstrations of a task, uses them to train and refine models, and evaluates the resulting behavior on KR1 before testing it in customer operations.The platform supports both Bear’s internally developed models and external foundation models. These models can learn patterns from training data and apply them to tasks involving different objects and environments.To run the software on KR1, Bear integrated NVIDIA Isaac OS into its perception system, which processes information about the robot’s surroundings. The setup uses NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor hardware and incorporates NVIDIA Holoscan SDK 5.0.Bear also used NVIDIA TensorRT and model quantization to reduce inference delays. Quantization makes models less computationally demanding by representing their numerical values with lower precision.According to Bear, these changes helped reduce NVIDIA Isaac GR00T inference time to approximately 60 milliseconds from an initially unoptimized 500 milliseconds. Its own model achieved a reduction from 72.3 to 17.2 milliseconds.Faster inference could help robots respond more quickly when identifying objects and deciding how to handle them. However, the announcement does not provide comparative data on complete task times, manipulation accuracy or long-term reliability.From demonstrations to deliveriesAt NVIDIA GTC Berlin, Bear is demonstrating KR1 performing a warehouse workflow that combines object handling and transportation.The robot receives an order from a warehouse management system, picks bottles, places them into a crate, delivers the crate to a drop-off point and returns with an empty one.The demonstration combines KINO-2’s learned manipulation skills with Bear’s existing navigation, control and workflow software.“The people doing a job already understand its products, equipment and sequence of work. Demonstrations let us capture that knowledge and teach the robot,” said Bren Pierce, Bear Robotics’ chief robotics officer.Bear says it is also developing manipulation capabilities through customer pilots involving supermarket returns and warehouse crate handling.The company plans to combine specialized mobile robots that transport goods with KR1 humanoids that handle objects. Both would operate through shared fleet-management and workflow systems.The GTC demonstration shows how these capabilities can work together in a defined warehouse task. Bear has not disclosed performance results establishing how reliably KR1 can complete broader customer workflows without intervention.

title: Tesla Optimus production starts as Musk targets 20,000 robots weekly
content: Tesla has begun manufacturing its Optimus humanoid robots on production lines in Fremont, California, marking a key step toward commercial deployment. CEO Elon Musk now aims to scale output to 20,000 robots per week by the end of 2027.The factory previously built electric vehicles, but Tesla has repurposed the manufacturing space for its robotics ambitions. The initial production run marks the first time Tesla has manufactured Optimus units to production standards. However, reaching mass production will require further engineering work and improvements to manufacturing efficiency.Tesla disclosed the milestone in its third-quarter 2026 shareholder update. Musk cautioned investors that production would ramp up slowly because Optimus represents an entirely new product category for the company.Tesla tackles robot manufacturingTesla has established a manufacturing process that it considers suitable for a commercial Optimus product. The company still expects to refine its production methods and robot hardware as manufacturing expands.Musk described the current phase as early production during Tesla’s earnings call. He warned that scaling output would involve setbacks as engineers address the challenges of building humanoid robots at industrial volumes.Q3 Shareholder Update → https://t.co/sXBSeLiJIjHighlights– FSD Supervised attach rate grew to over 75% of new vehicle deliveries in NA– Unveiled the next-gen Roadster– Record deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan & Taiwan– Tesla Semi now in volume production. Top… pic.twitter.com/yQQRq9LwSd— Tesla (@Tesla) October 21, 2026Reliability remains a major hurdle. Tesla wants Optimus to operate safely over extended periods without frequent repairs or component failures. Musk acknowledged that engineers still need to refine the robot’s design to meet those requirements.Software also presents a significant challenge. Tesla must develop the capabilities that allow Optimus to handle unfamiliar tasks reliably. Musk said considerable work remains before the robot can perform a broad range of activities independently.The planned production rate of 20,000 units per week would represent an ambitious manufacturing target. Achieving that volume would require Tesla to establish a supply chain and production system capable of supporting sustained output.Computing capacity supports roboticsTesla is also expanding its computing infrastructure to support autonomous driving and humanoid robot development. The company plans to reach 400 megawatts of training computing capacity by the end of 2026.That infrastructure will support software development for both its vehicles and Optimus robots. Tesla has also continued construction of its Austin fabrication facility, where equipment commissioning should begin in 2027.The computing expansion reflects the substantial processing demands involved in developing autonomous machines. Optimus needs to interpret its surroundings, plan movements, and execute tasks in changing environments.Tesla has yet to establish when Optimus will become commercially available at scale. Its production progress marks an important manufacturing milestone, but the robot’s practical capabilities remain a work in progress.Battery supply bottleneckTesla’s manufacturing ambitions extend beyond robotics. The automaker identified battery availability as a continuing constraint on its ability to increase global vehicle production.To address supply limitations, Tesla is expanding battery-related operations across several locations. Projects include battery pack capacity in Berlin, cathode material production and lithium refining in Texas, and lithium iron phosphate cell manufacturing in Nevada.Tesla has already shipped its first Megapack energy storage systems built exclusively with its own LFP cells. The milestone gives the company greater control over a key battery technology used in its energy storage business.Production of Tesla’s 4680 battery cells is also increasing. Those cells will support production ramps for the Cybertruck and Tesla Semi, alongside higher Model Y volumes.The robotics push arrives as Tesla faces pressure in its core automotive business. Third-quarter revenue reached $28.04 billion, nearly unchanged from $28.09 billion a year earlier. Profit fell 43% as expenses increased amid investments in robotics, computing infrastructure and autonomous driving.Tesla’s ability to turn Optimus into a reliable commercial product will depend on more than factory output. Manufacturing scale, battery availability, and software development must advance together before the robots can deliver on Musk’s ambitious production targets.

title: Archaeologists Discover Lost Roman Fort That Could Rewrite an Ancient Welsh Legend
content:
Archaeological excavations in west Wales have uncovered evidence of a previously unidentified Roman fort, potentially reshaping understanding of the region’s Roman occupation. Credit: Shutterstock
Pottery, coins, and buried defenses point to a Roman fort in west Wales, offering a possible setting for Emperor Magnus Maximus’s camp in medieval Welsh folklore.
My recent discovery of a Roman fort and its extraordinary connection with medieval folklore was the fruition of many hours of painstaking research.
This all began in 2002 when I discovered, or, more accurately, rediscovered, a Roman villa some 30 kilometers to the southwest of
. The site was first identified in the early 19th century by
Richard Fenton
, a local antiquarian. For several reasons, his reliability has been questioned, but mostly because of the perception that the Romans did not reach west Wales, which was rife in the Regency period and persists to this day.
When my team and I were digging the villa, a local volunteer asked what a Roman site of this status was doing in the middle of nowhere. This was a good question, and I did not know the answer. However, the archaeologist
Sir Mortimer Wheeler
dug a similar site on the same latitude in 1922, and I reasoned that both sites could lay close to a Roman road. This began a quest to trace a network of routes through west Wales.
A stretch of Roman road was in fact identified by Fenton in the vale of Whitland. This was excavated in 1995, in advance of the construction of a bypass, but I felt that there was more of a network to be discovered. I made a breakthrough in 2022. Several other Romano-British sites have been discovered since Wheeler’s day, including a fort at
near Haverfordwest in 2012–2013, and several villas.
Like Fenton, my observations have attracted a good deal of skepticism, but my heart and mind felt that I was making considerable progress tracing the Roman road network from Pembrokeshire east into Carmarthenshire.
My theory received a boost in 2024 with the observation of earthworks suggestive of a Roman auxiliary fort adjacent to an almost certain Roman road near Crymych in north Pembrokeshire. The earthworks had a characteristic playing-card shape like auxiliary forts and was about three hectares in area, which is typical for this type of military installation.
One corner has been destroyed by the construction of a post-medieval settlement (the village of Crymych), which is still inhabited today. The south of the enclosure is intersected by a leat (aqueduct) that enters the site through a masonry channel. Every Roman fort, of course, needed a water supply. The site lies adjacent to the A478, which runs straight in that area, and many sections further south are similar, but the line is lost in places, which is often the case with Roman roads.
It is my belief that it is part of a previously unidentified major arterial Roman road connecting modern Pembrokeshire with Ceredigion to the north.
My hypothesis gained traction with the results of a limited geophysical survey in October 2025, which placed two rectilinear (straight-lined and right-angled) buildings in the right place. Trial excavations followed in March and July 2025, and a steady trickle of finds followed, including coins, a gaming counter, some Roman pottery, and a spindle whorl for spinning wool. A more comprehensive evaluation excavation was needed, however, to establish for certain whether the site was a Roman auxiliary fort.
Connections to Welsh mythology
When I discovered the site in 2024, I began to think that it may relate to Cadair Maxen, the camp of the Roman emperor Magnus Maximus (Macsen Wledig in Welsh). He’s mentioned in the Mabinogion (a collection of medieval Welsh stories) in The Tale of Emperor Maxen, also known as
The Dream of Macsen Wledig
This places the late 4th-century usurping emperor on the Frenni Fawr, the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which dominates the site a little over three kilometers to the northeast. However, there are no visible remains of a Roman marching camp on the Frenni Fawr where the emperor is said to have visited.
Our breakthrough came in early September with the excavation of five trenches. Three across the suspected principal buildings (the commander’s house, headquarters building, and granaries); one in the area to the north where a perimeter road would be expected; and another up-slope where the geophysical survey (non-invasive ground scans detecting buried stone structures and drainage ditches beneath the soil) indicated a track.
In the first and second trenches, we identified the bases of floor structures built of clay and packed with the remnants of thin stone blocks. Many of the latter had been disturbed by intermittent plowing over many decades.
In the second trench there was a diagonal alignment of stones, which indicated a later phase of civilian occupation. We recovered many pottery sherds, particularly in the second trench, and found a kiln, which yielded many fragments of Roman ceramic tile.
The third trench had a clay floor consistent with Roman granaries. In the fourth trench we unearthed the remnants of the rampart base and a road surface below plow level with rut marks on their expected orientation. The fifth trench did indeed reveal a track. Its date has yet to be established, but we did recover a small number of pottery sherds that are seemingly Roman.
Other new finds from the site include a lead spindle-whorl, an iron stylus for writing documents and letters on wax tablets, a woodworking axe, a gaming counter, a third-century coin, and two later fourth-century coins.
The collective findings indicate that the site was once a typical timber fort, probably established during the campaign of the governor Sextus Julius Frontinus between AD 74 and 78. It does indeed suggest a connection between the camp of Magnus Maximus mentioned in the Mabinogion and the site I first identified in 2024. Magnus Maximus will feature in my forthcoming book,
Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus
The earthworks are still visible today, almost certainly adjacent to a major Roman road, and would have been more conspicuous in the 4th century and listed on official itineraries. The discovery represents an extraordinary fusion between myth and reality and demonstrates that folklore is often underpinned by fact.

title: These Mysterious Underwater Reefs Could Help Save Marine Life As Coral Reefs Decline
content:
Peat reef habitat fauna, a bluebanded snapper. Credit: Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory
Submerged ancient forest floors off Mozambique now shelter young reef fish, suggesting overlooked peat reefs could offer some species refuge as coral reefs decline.
Much of the seabed along Mozambique’s Bazaruto coastline is shifting sand, leaving marine life few solid places to settle and shelter. Exposed layers of ancient peat provide that foothold, supporting fish communities comparable in diversity to those on a nearby coral reef.
These submerged “peat reefs” began as coastal swamps and forests. Their plant remains accumulated into peat, a compressed, carbon-rich material. As sea levels rose over the past few thousand years, the sea flooded these landscapes. Waves later stripped away the overlying sand, exposing firm platforms that marine life could colonize.
A study published in
Scientific Reports
documents these habitats in the shallow waters of the Bazaruto Archipelago in the Western Indian Ocean. Researchers from the Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory worked with collaborators at universities and research institutions in the United Kingdom, United States, and Canada. The work is believed to be the first ecological study of tropical peat reefs and the first anywhere to examine peat reefs from a biodiversity perspective.
Peat reef habitat exposed by the tides. Credit: Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory
A fish nursery without living coral
The team surveyed three peat reefs and a nearby coral reef, comparing seabed cover, invertebrates, small fish, and larger animals such as sharks, rays, and turtles. No living coral grew on the peat reefs. Instead, seagrass and seaweeds grew directly on the peat, while crevices and ledges sheltered spiny lobsters, oysters, barnacles, and juvenile fish. Young snappers and grunts, usually associated with coral reefs, likely use these spaces as refuges from predators.
Each peat reef supported 26 to 36 small fish species, with species diversity comparable to the coral reef. The two reef types shared much of their fish life, even though their communities of invertebrates attached to the seabed were entirely different. Sharks, rays, and turtles were also recorded on both reef types. Green turtles and dugongs occur in the area and could graze the seagrass patches, although that potential role remains distinct from the animals documented during the surveys.
Marine life inhabiting submerged peat reefs in the Bazaruto Archipelago. Crevices and ledges in the ancient peat provide shelter for juvenile fish and invertebrates, creating biodiversity-rich habitats without living coral. Credit: Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory
“What was once a forest floor is now a nursery for reef fish. We were surprised by how much life these ancient peat deposits support, and how many species move between them and the coral reefs nearby. This coastline has very little natural hard seabed, mostly shifting sand. When rising seas expose these old peat layers, they create rare, solid habitat where marine life can settle, hide and feed,” said Dr. Mario Lebrato, lead author and co-founder of the BCSS Ocean Observatory.
The research was enabled by the observatory’s monitoring capabilities, described in two earlier papers in
Frontiers in Marine Science
. Established in Mozambique’s Bazaruto Archipelago in 2017, BCSS is Africa’s first permanent Ocean Observatory. It has generated more than 22 million measurements across over 30 chemical, environmental, and biodiversity variables.
Radiocarbon dating results from peat samples collected in the Bazaruto Archipelago, providing evidence of ancient terrestrial vegetation deposits formed over approximately the past 5,000 years. Credit: Lebrato et al. (2026), Scientific Reports
Its network spans six interconnected ecosystems and 14 long-term monitoring stations across approximately 6,850 square kilometers, or 2,645 square miles, of the greater Bazaruto seascape. The habitats monitored range from mangroves and seagrass meadows to peat and coral reefs, lagoons, seamounts, and the open ocean.
Storms bury and break apart peat reefs
The peat reefs occupy a particularly changeable part of that seascape. Sitting just 2–4 meters deep, or about 7–13 feet, they are regularly exposed by the tides and receive much more sunlight than the deeper coral reef. Temperatures can shift between 24.5 and 28.6°C, or 76.1 and 83.5°F, within a day. Storms and cyclones bury, uncover, and break apart the peat, and many reefs disappear through erosion and sand movement as sea levels continue to rise.
“The existence of tropical peat reefs underscores the resilience and adaptive reinvention potential of coastal ecosystems under pressure from sea-level rise and shoreline change. Their contribution to biodiversity, fisheries habitat, and potential legacy-carbon preservation should be recognized in coastal management and conservation strategies, particularly in regions where coral reef health is declining. The ability to demonstrate the vitality of these habitats as a result of our continuous observation excites me for the prospect of implementing conservation policy that protects similar regions around the world,” Lebrato said.
A scientific survey quadrat positioned over a coral reef in the Bazaruto Archipelago, Mozambique. Standardised sampling methods allow researchers to document reef communities and compare biodiversity across coral and peat reef habitats. Credit: Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory
Peat reefs’ carbon balance remains unknown
Radiocarbon, or carbon-14, dating places the formation of the peat between roughly 300 and 5,000 years ago. Chemical analysis confirms that it came mostly from coastal land plants and trees, and some samples contained up to 40% organic carbon by dry weight. Ancient plant carbon has persisted beneath the sea for thousands of years, but the amount held across these reefs remains unknown.
For comparison, peat swamps on land can hold 1,000–2,000 metric tons of carbon per hectare below ground. That does not establish how much carbon the submerged reefs contain, or whether they are storing or releasing carbon today.
Ancient peat deposits along Mozambique’s Bazaruto coastline. Once part of terrestrial forests and coastal wetlands, these carbon-rich formations now provide hard underwater surfaces that support marine life. Credit: Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory
Resolving those questions requires measurements of peat thickness and bulk density, which describes how much material occupies a given volume. Researchers also need to determine carbon stocks per unit area, the rates at which peat is buried or eroded, and the movement of greenhouse gases into and out of these systems. Without those measurements, the reefs’ present-day role in carbon cycling remains unresolved.
Scientists have spent decades examining how warming and disturbance affect ancient carbon in tundra, peatlands, and mangroves. Tropical peat reefs are at a much earlier stage of understanding. Their discovery raises related questions beneath the sea about how stable the stored carbon is and what happens when the deposits erode or are disturbed.
Comparison of surveyed peat reef and coral reef habitats in the Bazaruto Archipelago, combining aerial imagery and underwater photographs to illustrate their contrasting structures and marine environments. Credit: Lebrato et al. (2026), Scientific Reports
The authors call for research to establish whether these habitats primarily preserve carbon inherited from ancient forests and swamps, whether their living communities contribute to new carbon burial, and how those processes interact as environmental conditions change. The answers would help determine whether peat reefs can be classified as “blue carbon” habitats alongside mangroves and seagrass meadows.
Coastal planners and conservationists rarely map or protect peat reefs, despite their potential to provide backup refuges for some species as coral reefs decline. The authors recommend including them in coastal habitat maps, conservation plans, and assessments of legacy coastal carbon. They also see the study as a starting point for considering these habitats within broader blue economy policies governing the use and protection of ocean resources. Similar peat reefs may lie undiscovered along the coasts of Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and West Africa.
Reference: “Ancient terrestrial forests reborn as modern marine ecosystems under shifting sea levels” by Mario Lebrato, Jack Shannon, Theo Russell, Alexandra Jordan, Mauro Jije-Goncalves, Maria da Graça, Michelle Caputo and Ashlee Lillis, 12 October 2026,
Scientific Reports
DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-65430-7
Funding was provided by the Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS)-Kisawa Sanctuary (Mozambique) resort-to-research (R2R) initiative.

title: Scientists Discover “D-Rex,” a Giant Fungus Unlike Anything Seen Before
content:
Nicknamed “D-Rex,” Dianjunus rex is a newly discovered giant fungus found in China’s forests. Reaching up to 20 inches tall and weighing nearly 5 pounds, it produces the largest known fruiting bodies of any fungus in its group. Credit: Kunming Institute of Botany / Chinese Academy of Sciences
A newly discovered giant fungus belongs to a previously unknown family that may have emerged around 65 million years ago, shortly after the mass extinction that killed the non-avian dinosaurs.
A fungus discovered in China’s Yunnan forests produces whitish, spore-bearing structures up to 50 centimeters (about 20 inches) tall and weighing as much as 2.2 kilograms (4.9 pounds). The newly described species,
Dianjunus rex
, has the largest known fruiting bodies in the fungal phylum Ascomycota, surpassing previous record holders that stood 20 to 30 centimeters (about 8 to 12 inches) tall.
Ascomycota is the largest group of fungi, with more than 64,000 species. Its members, called ascomycetes, do not grow true mushrooms. Instead, they release spores from tiny, sac-like structures inside or on the surfaces of their fruiting bodies. For
, producing such large reproductive structures could offer an advantage in a crowded forest, although the researchers have not established why it grows so big.
“A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests. However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs,” hypothesized Dr. Indunil C Senanayake, the study’s corresponding author and an associate professor at the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species of the Kunming Institute of Botany in China.
DNA reveals a new fungal family
Scientists from the institute encountered the fungus during fieldwork in temperate coniferous forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang and in tropical rainforest near Nanbang. Its upright fruiting bodies, known as stromata, grew on the woody roots of Chinese cork oak, emerging from the rhizosphere, the soil immediately surrounding the roots. Senanayake said, “The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests.”
To investigate what they had found, the researchers collected fruiting bodies and deposited voucher specimens in the Kunming Institute of Botany’s collections. They grew spores on laboratory media to study the fungus’s form and structure and sequenced its genome, including its full set of protein-coding genes.
Stromata of Dianjunus rex in the field. (a, c, d, f) Stromata attached to host roots. (b, e, g, h) Stromata around host plant. (a) Collectors. (i) Total weight of largest bilobedstromata. Credit: Song, Yan, Pérez-Moreno, Zhang, Yang, Xie, Su, Liu, Wang, Liu, Yang, Yang, Liu, Shi, Wan, Cheewangkoon, Dai, Senanayake and Yu
The genetic results, supported by the detailed examination of its morphology, established a new species and genus within the order Xylariales. The findings, published in
Frontiers in Fungal Biology
, also warranted recognition at a broader level of classification.
“This remarkable species represents a new fungal family, Dianjunaceae, and provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms,” said Senanayake.
The researchers chose the name
Dianjunus rex
for the fungus’s regal size and the ancient Dian kingdom. Its closest known relative,
Graphostroma platystoma
, grows on dead hardwood across the Northern Hemisphere and is itself the sole member of another family, Graphostromataceae.
Mass extinction may have favored wood-decomposing fungi
Other fungi in Xylariales are known for producing secondary compounds, chemicals beyond those essential for basic growth, as well as enzymes that break down complex plant molecules. Similar enzymes might help “D-rex” digest dead wood, a possibility that gives context to the researchers’ investigation of its evolutionary origins.
Using a molecular clock analysis, which estimates evolutionary timing from genetic differences, the team compared the new species’ DNA with genomes from hundreds of fungi with known evolutionary ages. The results suggested that the Dianjunaceae family arose around 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. That event wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and countless other animals and plants.
“This timing raises an intriguing possibility. After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material,” said Senanayake. “For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities.”
The researchers expect more fungal discoveries in subtropical China, where conditions favor diversification but finding and documenting species remains difficult.
“This region combines exceptional habitat heterogeneity, climatic stability, and complex biotic interactions that promote fungal diversification. Historically, however, fungal diversity in these ecosystems has been underestimated due to logistical difficulties in field sampling, the seasonal and cryptic nature of fungal fruiting, and a historical emphasis on economically important fungi,” said Senanayake.
Reference: “Unearthing a fungal giant: Dianjunaceae fam. nov., a novel Paleocene lineage of Xylariales harboring Dianjunus rex gen. et sp. nov” by Jing Song, Zhuyue Yan, Jesús Pérez-Moreno, Fengming Zhang, Shimei Yang, Tao Xie, Luofeng Su, Jianwei Liu, Yanliang Wang, Dong Liu, Zhenyan Yang, Chengmo Yang, Wei Liu, Xiaofei Shi, Shanping Wan, Ratchadawan Cheewangkoon, Dongqin Dai, Indunil C. Senanayake and Fuqiang Yu, 8 September 2026,
Frontiers in Fungal Biology
DOI: 10.3389/ffunb.2026.1940464

title: Scientists Develop a Remarkable New Coating for the Powerhouses of Our Cells
content:
Chemistry
Coating mitochondria with Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOF) may help them performing specific functions, while still retaining their ability to produce energy. Credit: Politecnico di Milano
Scientists have given the tiny powerhouses of our cells a remarkable high-tech makeover that preserves their energy production and could pave the way for future treatments.
Scientists have developed a way to coat mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing energy inside cells, with advanced materials without interfering with their ability to function. The breakthrough could eventually help researchers develop new approaches to treating diseases caused by malfunctioning mitochondria.
The discovery comes from a collaboration between IRCCS Fondazione Istituto Neurologico Carlo Besta (FINCB) and Politecnico di Milano. The work was conducted through the BraiNs joint laboratory and published in the
Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS)
The project combines the expertise of two research teams. One is led by Dr. Valeria Tiranti (FINCB), who works in the Medical Genetics and Neurogenetics Complex Unit (SC) and heads the Fondazione Mariani Center for Pediatric Mitochondrial Diseases. The other is led by Professor Pierangelo Metrangolo (Politecnico di Milano), whose team specializes in chemistry and materials engineering.
Why Mitochondria Are So Important
Often described as the powerhouses of cells, mitochondria generate the energy needed to keep essential cellular processes running. When they malfunction, they can contribute to a range of medical conditions, including rare mitochondrial diseases.
These disorders are particularly harmful to tissues that require large amounts of energy, such as the brain and muscles. Treatment options remain limited, making new strategies for working with mitochondria especially valuable.
The researchers focused on a class of advanced materials known as Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOF). These materials can be customized for different purposes by adjusting their properties. Their scientific importance was recognized with the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi.
A New Coating That Keeps Mitochondria Working
Applying these materials to mitochondria presents a considerable challenge because the cellular structures are extremely delicate. Even small changes to their surroundings could potentially interfere with their essential functions.
To overcome this difficulty, the researchers developed a technique that allows them to apply very small quantities of the materials directly to the mitochondrial surface.
Most importantly, the mitochondria continued producing energy after receiving the coating. This demonstrates that their surfaces can be modified with these materials without compromising their energy generating function.
Could This Breakthrough Lead to New Treatments?
The ability to customize the coating could make the technique useful for a variety of future applications. By changing the material’s properties, researchers may eventually be able to create coatings designed to carry out specific tasks.
“The possibility of modifying the coating now opens up new research prospects: in the future, it will be possible to develop MOF with different characteristics depending on the objective, creating coatings capable of performing specific functions,” observes Prof. Metrangolo.
One potential application involves mitochondrial transplantation, an experimental strategy that seeks to introduce healthy mitochondria into cells whose existing mitochondria are not functioning properly.
“A specifically designed coating could, in the future, facilitate this transfer and the interaction between mitochondria and cells,” emphasizes Dr. Tiranti.
Although the findings offer a promising direction for further research, the potential benefits for mitochondrial transplantation have not yet been demonstrated. Additional experiments will be necessary to establish whether coated mitochondria perform better during transplantation than those without coatings.

title: A Single Gene Could Hold the Key to Taming One of the Deadliest Cancers
content:
Scientists have uncovered how pancreatic cancer cells evolve into more aggressive forms, revealing genetic changes that may contribute to tumor spread and treatment resistance. Credit: Shutterstock
Blocking one gene’s activity shifted aggressive pancreatic cancer cells into a less aggressive form in experiments, pointing to a possible way to disrupt tumor evolution.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma kills nearly 85 percent of people within five years of diagnosis. Part of the challenge is that its cancer cells can change, shifting between less aggressive and more aggressive forms in ways that earlier studies could not explain.
A study led by researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center now shows how genetic reshaping within individual tumors enables those transitions. Published in
Nature Genetics
, the findings suggest that ongoing changes to cancer cells’ DNA help fuel both resistance to treatment and metastasis, the spread of cancer to other parts of the body.
Cancer clones follow different evolutionary paths
More than half a dozen genes have been implicated in this complex disease. Earlier research generally measured increases and decreases in gene activity across groups of cells analyzed together, separating pancreatic cancer cells into two broad subtypes: classical, which is less aggressive, and basal, which is more aggressive. Those bulk measurements could not explain how cells switched between the two.
To examine the differences among individual cells, the researchers used transcriptomics, which measures gene activity. They analyzed 443,451 single cells from 62 tumors in 56 men and women with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Six patients provided tumor samples both before and after chemotherapy, allowing the team to examine changes across treatment.
“Our study provides the most granular view to date of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, revealing how ongoing genetic reshaping drives tumor evolution over the course of disease,” said study lead investigator Despoina Kalfakakou, PhD, a postdoctoral research fellow at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and Perlmutter Cancer Center.
Within the tumors, the team identified clones, groups of cells with similar genetic makeup. Individual tumors contained between two and 11 clones on average, with mixtures of basal and classical cells. These groups behaved differently as they evolved, with some developing resistance to therapy and others acquiring the ability to spread rapidly.
“Our research also suggests that single-cell clonal analysis offers a better approach to understanding complex cancers, like pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, as it develops over time, by mapping how tumors evolve and adapt at each stage of disease progression,” said study co-senior investigator Aristotelis Tsirigos, PhD, a professor in the Departments of Medicine and Pathology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a member of Perlmutter Cancer Center.
Blocking MYC reverses an aggressive state
Using patterns of gene activity to trace the clones’ genetic origins, the researchers linked variations in DNA copy number to the mix of cells making up each tumor. This helped them identify which genes were most active at different stages of disease progression. Among the changes associated with tumor evolution was increased activity of a gene called MYC in aggressive tumor cell populations.
In further experiments with basal pancreatic tumor cells, blocking MYC activity returned the cells to the less aggressive classical form. It also exposed them to more immune cells, potentially making them more vulnerable to immune attack. “These findings suggest that targeting the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, including MYC, may help restrain the cancer’s rapid progression,” Kalfakakou said.
Clues to pancreatic cancer’s immune escape
Other differences among clones offered clues to why this cancer resists immunotherapy. In some clones, the TIGIT gene was more active, producing proteins that help cancer evade immune detection. In those same cells, activity of the PD1 gene was suppressed, which may help explain why some immunotherapies targeting PD1 are rarely effective against the disease.
“More broadly, our study results highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, genetic plasticity, and interactions with the tumor’s microenvironment in shaping human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma biology,” said Dr. Tsirigos, who also serves as co-director of the Division of Precision Medicine and director of NYU Langone’s Applied Bioinformatics Laboratories.
Clinical trials of MYC inhibitors or TIGIT inhibitors for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other cancers are underway, Tsirigos said. He added that the findings should encourage larger investigations into the different states cancer cells can occupy and how treatments might target them.

title: Scientists Discover That One Common Protein Source Makes Gut Inflammation Much Worse
content:
Researchers have uncovered a potential connection between dietary protein, gut microbes, and intestinal inflammation that could reshape future approaches to managing inflammatory bowel disease. Credit: Shutterstock
A diet’s protein source may influence how severely the gut becomes inflamed, with mouse experiments offering clues for more tailored dietary guidance for people with inflammatory bowel disease.
The protein on your plate may do more than build muscle. Growing evidence suggests that where dietary protein comes from could influence inflammation in the gut, raising important questions about how food choices might affect people living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
IBD includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic conditions in which abnormal immune responses contribute to ongoing inflammation in the digestive tract. Symptoms can include persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue, and intestinal bleeding, often alternating between periods of remission and unpredictable flare-ups. Although genetics, immune function, and gut microbes all play important roles, researchers are still working to understand how diet influences the disease.
IBD has also become increasingly common in the United States and worldwide over recent decades, alongside shifts in dietary habits that include greater consumption of animal protein. Despite these trends, scientists have yet to establish clear, evidence-based recommendations about which protein sources might be most beneficial for people with IBD.
As the authors explain, “Although diet is believed to be an important contributor to the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel diseases, there are few evidence-based dietary recommendations for patients to lessen disease severity.”
Milder inflammation in mice fed pea protein
A new study in
Cellular and Molecular Gastroenterology
explored whether the source of dietary protein could change the severity of intestinal inflammation. Researchers compared diets containing beef, egg, dairy, soy, or pea protein across multiple mouse models of IBD.
Mice fed beef protein consistently developed the most severe intestinal inflammation, while those consuming pea protein experienced the least inflammation and only mild symptoms. The pattern remained consistent across the different models and in both male and female mice.
“Mice fed a beef protein diet exhibited the most severe colitis, whereas mice fed pea protein developed mild inflammation,” the authors say.
Importantly, beef protein alone did not cause overt intestinal inflammation in mice without a colitis trigger, suggesting that its effects depend on other factors involved in the disease.
Mice fed a beef-protein diet developed the most severe intestinal inflammation, while those consuming pea protein experienced only mild symptoms. Credit: CMGH
Gut microbes may connect diet and inflammation
The findings point to interactions between gut microbes, the intestinal barrier, and bile acids as a possible explanation for the differences. The intestinal barrier helps separate the gut’s contents from surrounding tissue, while bile acids help digest fats. How microbes interact with that barrier and those acids appears to influence whether these processes promote or reduce inflammation.
“The colitis-promoting effects of beef protein were microbially mediated,” the authors say.
Further experiments revealed that beef protein altered the balance of intestinal bacteria and was associated with a thinner protective mucus layer and higher levels of certain bile acids linked to inflammation. In contrast, pea protein supported a different microbial balance and bile acid profile.
The authors also found that adding psyllium, a soluble dietary fiber, to the beef-protein diet reduced inflammation in mice, suggesting that other dietary components may help counteract some of these effects.
Protein choices could become a focus of future dietary guidance aimed at helping people manage IBD and reducing disease risk and severity.
“These findings provide a rationale for determining whether modifying dietary protein source could lessen the severity of disease in patients with inflammatory bowel diseases,” the authors say.
